# Roadmap

## v0.3 (done 2026-10-01): a usable, documented language
1. Land in-flight work (local imports, partial stdlib packages, agent-reported compiler bugs). Done.
2. Robustness: panic backtraces, bounds failures with index and length, defer. Done.
3. Remaining stdlib: stamp, seal, ore, flume, herald, wire, crucible. Done.
4. Docs: docs/LANGUAGE.md, docs/STDLIB.md (generated), README. Done.
5. Final benchmarks (README). Done.

## Linux port (done 2026-10-01)
linux-arm64 and linux-amd64 pass every suite and self-host; CI runs all three targets
natively. All review issues (#1–#21, #43, #44) are fixed.

## Next milestone: Tin 1 (decided 2026-10-04)
The server language of the design brief: one semantic model (notes/design_semantics.md) and a
new syntax that replaces v0.5's Go syntax (notes/design_syntax.md). Order:
1. Edition-1 parser, the `tin fix -edition 1` translator, one commit converting the repository,
   the old parser removed; LANGUAGE.md, AGENT_PRIMER.md, README and examples rewritten
   (design_syntax §12, §14; about 4 PRs).
2. The semantic steps of design_semantics §16, in the new syntax (about 30 PRs): fault chains,
   unwinding and `guard`, boundary records and cancellation, `scope`/`parallel`/`select`/`detach`,
   `within`, safepoints, `limit`, long-lived reclamation (#176), `arena`/`once`, `with`, `use`/`on`
   and the lifecycle, `secret`, bounded values, production replay, diagnostic codes.
3. `selfhost/` moved to the new syntax.
These supersede the overlapping parts of design_foundations.md (design_semantics §14) and the
"Foundations" checklist below where they differ.

## v0.5: syntax (notes/syntax_v05.md, superseded by notes/design_syntax.md; phases 2–8 of #46)
Go syntax kept; adds `!T`/`fail`/`catch`, call-site `mut`, `for i := range n`, the
capitalized-export rule, string interpolation, enums with exhaustive `switch`, more map key
types with insertion order, `f32`, and Go-style `*_test.tin` tests.

## v0.4: non-blocking I/O inside handlers (design in notes/design_v04.md; phases 9–13 of #46)
From the user's spec (2026-10-01):
- Stackful tasks per in-flight request on each core; waiting on a socket registers the fd with
  the core's kqueue and switches to the event loop; resume when ready. Pooled task stacks with
  guard pages; cap in-flight requests per core (backpressure).
- Request pool moves from per-core to per-request; each request's pool is wiped when it
  finishes; the region checker still forbids escapes without keep().
- Non-blocking outbound TCP client; Redis client (pooled per core, pipelined); MySQL client
  (wire protocol, prepared statements, pooled per core); every call takes a timeout and a
  deadline cancels the request.
- Small pool of blocking helper threads (file I/O, DNS) reporting back via relay.
Done when: a 100ms-wait handler on a core does not delay fast requests on that core; GET
/users/{id} via Redis cache backed by MySQL, wrk2 vs the same service in Go with chi: Tin wins
on req/s and p99, including a slow/fast mix. make bootstrap stays a fixed point, tests green.
Show the design (task switching, stack size, pool ownership) before building.

Status (2026-10-02): phases 9–12 and the websocket package are merged (#64–#73): request
tasks, non-blocking I/O and helper threads, `query`, redis, mysql, websocket. Phase 13's
service and harness are in bench/v04 (Tin and Go + chi, wrk2); the final measurement on a
quiet machine is still to do (see the open benchmark issue).

## Foundations (decided 2026-10-02): notes/design_foundations.md
Closures that capture, shapes, fault chains and `guard`, tasks and scopes with `context` as ambient
deadline and cancellation, atomics, compile-time type information, packages with capabilities. The
document decides each, with what it replaces, what was rejected and what it unlocks, and orders the
nine steps by dependency. docs/COVERAGE.md is the checklist of what each adds.


## Ten-year plan (written 2026-10-02)

Tin's goal: a language as ready as Go, Rust and Odin for servers and tools, written in Tin, with
performance as the end goal. This is the whole list, ordered by phase; a box is checked when it is merged
with its tests (and, for library work, verified against Go: see notes/stdlib_verified.md). Years are targets,
not promises; the order inside a phase follows dependencies (notes/design_foundations.md). The standard
library checklist (section 9) is generated from notes/coverage.md; docs/COVERAGE.md is its
published generated inventory.

### 1. Language (year 1 to 3)

Every item below follows the template of 12.1 (design note, parser, checker, codegen on arm64 and amd64, tests, docs, stdlib adoption, performance check). Each explanation names the work, why Tin needs it, the approach, what it waits on, and the test that closes it.

Foundations, in the order of notes/design_foundations.md (#140 to #146):
- [x] Closures that capture, as region objects with cells (#140)
  **Work:** let a function literal read and write any variable in scope; the closure becomes a region object (code pointer plus a table of one-word cells allocated in the current region), and both the closure and its parent hold the cells, so writes are shared as in Go. **Why:** today literals are lifted to top-level functions and cannot capture (LANGUAGE.md section 3, "Function values"), so every callback needs a hand-written state struct, anvil middleware has to thread `next` through `Out`, and the `Func` forms of `sift` and `twine` cannot carry state; design_foundations section 1 puts closures first because scopes, callbacks and most of the library depend on them. **How:** capture analysis in `check.tin`/`lower.tin` decides which locals become cells, `func$N` lifting gains an environment parameter, a function value becomes code pointer plus environment (a top-level function gets a null environment), the region checker treats the closure as an allocation in its region, `keep(f)` deep-copies code pointer and cells, and a closure that never escapes keeps its cells in the frame (no allocation). **Needs:** nothing (step 1 of design_foundations section 9). **Done when:** `sift.Each(xs, func(x i64) { total += x })` and a counter closure work on all three targets, storing a capturing closure in a global without `keep` is a compile error naming the variable, the frame-local optimization is measured to allocate zero bytes for a non-escaping closure, and `make bootstrap` stays a fixed point.
- [x] Shapes: structural interfaces, static by default, `dyn` for dynamic dispatch (#141)
  **Work:** add `shape` declarations (sets of method signatures, composable by listing shapes, plus named unions such as `shape Ordered = i64 | ... | str`), structural satisfaction with no `impl` declaration, use as a type-parameter constraint (monomorphized, the default), and `dyn S` as a two-word fat reference (object pointer plus a static method table). **Why:** `io.Reader`/`Writer`, `hash.Hash`, `database/sql/driver`, `fmt.Stringer` and `net.Conn` have no Tin form without a way to write code over "anything with these methods" (design_foundations section 2); Tin has no interfaces by design, and shapes keep "nothing hidden" because dispatch is only dynamic where `dyn` is written. **How:** extend `generics.tin` so a constraint can be a shape checked at instantiation, then add `dyn` conversion at assignment sites that builds a per-(type, shape) table in writable data filled at startup; no downcast, no type switch, no runtime type information; `?dyn S` is the optional. **Needs:** nothing (step 2), but generic-constraint work (below) shares code. **Done when:** `func Copy[R Reader, W Writer]` and `func Log(w dyn Writer, ...)` compile and run on all targets, a missing or mis-signed method gives a diagnostic with the method name and a fix-it, `dyn` calls cost one indirect call and zero allocations in a benchmark, and `any`, `comparable` and `Ordered` are library names rather than syntax.
- [ ] Fault chains: `fault.Is`, `Wrap`, `Join`, `try ... wrap`, sentinels, `guard` in place of `recover` (#142)
  **Work:** make a fault a value holding a message and an optional cause; package-level `fault("...")` values become sentinels with identity; add the `fault` package (`Wrap`, `Is`, `Cause`, `Join`, `Message`), the `try E wrap "msg"` sugar, and `guard CALL`, which runs a call in a sub-region and turns a panic into a fault. **Why:** `errors` is one of the most imported packages in services and a fault today is only a message pointer (RUNTIME.md section 1), so callers cannot test for "not found" without comparing strings; `guard` gives per-request isolation (a bug in one handler must not kill the server) without `recover`'s invisible control flow (design_foundations section 3). There is deliberately no `fault.As` and no typed payload: structured results are enums. **How:** change the fault layout from a str pointer to a small record (message, cause, sentinel identity), keep `nil` as no fault, lower `wrap` in `lower_try_stmt`, implement `guard` with the unwinding design of 14.2 (run defers, run cleanup callbacks, rewind the pool to a mark), and wrap every anvil handler in `guard`. **Needs:** nothing for the chain; `guard` needs the unwinding design in 14.2. **Done when:** `fault.Is` walks wrapped and joined chains in tests, messages read `outer: inner`, a panicking anvil handler yields a logged 500 while other requests on the core continue (a `task_check.py`-style CI check), and the existing `!T` tests and fault messages compared with Go (link, mint) are unchanged.
- [ ] Tasks and scopes: `scope`, `spawn`, `lane[T]` (structured concurrency on a core) (#143)
  **Work:** let a program start child tasks inside a `scope` block that waits for all of them, with `s.spawn(f)`, `t.Wait() !T`, `s.cancel`, `s.yield()`, the bounded queue `lane[T]` (`New`, `Send`, `Recv`, `Close`) and `wait.First` over lanes and timeouts. **Why:** the runtime already runs each request as a stackful task that parks on I/O (RUNTIME.md, "Request tasks"), but user code cannot start a second one, so there is no fan-out inside a request and no replacement for `go`, `chan`, `select`, `sync.WaitGroup` or `errgroup` (design_foundations section 5). Children run on the parent's core and switch only where they park, which is why tasks never race and why no mutex exists; there is no detached `go`, no work stealing across cores and no preemption. **How:** build on `rt_task_run`, `rt_task_park`/`wake`/`defer`, the per-core ready queue and timer heap; a scope is a runtime record with a child list and a first-fault slot; children share the parent's region, which the region checker allows because the scope outlives them; the first child fault cancels siblings by waking their waits with `fault.Canceled`. **Needs:** closures (task bodies capture) and fault chains (`fault.Canceled`, scope faults). **Done when:** the `fetchAll` example of design_foundations section 5 runs with overlapping waits, a child fault cancels the others within one event-loop turn, a task cannot escape its scope (compile error), and conformance tests for ordering, cancellation, panics in children and timers pass on all targets.
- [ ] `context` as ambient deadline, cancellation and slots: `within`, `slot`/`with` (#144)
  **Work:** give every task an ambient deadline, an ambient cancellation and ambient typed slots inherited by the tasks it spawns: `within 2s { ... }` narrows the deadline, `slot requestID str` declares a typed key, `with requestID = v { ... }` binds it for a block, and `task.Canceled()` lets CPU-bound loops poll. **Why:** `context` is the most-imported package in the yardstick service (design_foundations section 4) and `ctx` is the first parameter of most Go functions; in Tin the deadline already belongs to the request task, so making it ambient removes a parameter from most signatures and the bug of a forgotten `ctx` that makes a call uncancellable. **How:** extend `rt_task_wait` (the one wait primitive) to also wake on scope cancellation; store deadline, cancel flag and slot bindings in the task record; `within` computes `min(now + d, current)`; slots are typed, hold only `keep`able values and cannot outlive their `with` block (region rule); reading an unset slot is a fault, not a nil. There is no untyped `Value()` and no `Background()` default. **Needs:** tasks and scopes. **Done when:** a `db.Query` inside `within 50ms` against a slow server fails with `fault.DeadlineExceeded` after about 50 ms, cancelling a scope wakes a task parked in `wire`, `redis`, `mysql`, `postgres` and `tide.Wait` with `fault.Canceled` without changes to those packages, and a slot read in a spawned child sees the parent's binding.
- [ ] Derivation and attributes in place of `reflect` and struct tags (#145)
  **Work:** add declared, compiler-checked attributes on fields (`@json("id")`, declared with `attr json(name str, omitempty bool)` by the package that interprets them) and compile-time iteration over a type's fields (`for f in fields[T]`, `v.field(f)`, `f.attr("json")`), unrolled per instantiation. **Why:** `reflect` and struct tags carry serialization, validation, row mapping and flag parsing in Go; Tin has no runtime type information by design ("nothing hidden"), and today `argo` and `say` are special cases inside `lower.tin`, so every new format would be a compiler change (design_foundations section 7). **How:** expose field name, type, offset and attributes in `generics.tin` as a compile-time list; unroll the loop when a generic function is instantiated; type-check attribute arguments against their `attr` declaration; then rewrite `argo` and `say`'s struct printing on the mechanism and delete the special cases. **Needs:** shapes (derived encoders are reached through shape constraints); generics. **Done when:** `argo.Put`/`Get` are ordinary library code generated through `fields[T]` with no regression on the bench/v2 JSON benchmark (1.08 s today), a misspelled attribute option is a compile error at the type declaration, and a binary that uses no derivation contains no type tables.
- [x] Packages with `tin.lock`, content addressing and capabilities (#146)
  **Work:** import packages by path (`import "github.com/ana/geo"`), record every dependency with a content hash in `tin.lock`, copy them into `vendor/` with `tin vendor`, build only from `vendor/`, and let each package's manifest declare capabilities (`net`, `files`, `spawn`, `exec`, `unsafe`) that the compiler enforces. **Why:** today a program can only import `lib/` packages by name and `./` local packages (COVERAGE, "modules"), so no third-party code exists; capabilities are the Tin-specific reason to build this: code generated or pulled in without review should not silently reach the network or the file system (design_foundations section 8). **How:** extend the package resolver in `selfhost/main.tin`; the lock file pins exact content hashes (no semantic version resolution, no central registry first); the build refuses a file whose hash differs; each `extern` or runtime entry point is tagged with the capability it needs and calls are checked transitively. **Needs:** nothing (step 9). **Done when:** a two-package program with a vendored dependency builds offline, editing one byte of a vendored file fails the build with the file and hash named, and a dependency that calls `wire.Dial` without the `net` capability is rejected at compile time with the call site.
- [ ] The `io` family on shapes (Reader, Writer, Closer, Seeker, ReaderAt, WriterTo)
  **Work:** declare the `io` shapes in a library package and port `Copy`, `CopyN`, `ReadAll`, `ReadFull`, `Pipe`, `MultiWriter`, `MultiReader`, `LimitReader`, `TeeReader`, `SectionReader` and `Discard`, then make `flume`, `wire.Conn`, files and the hashes satisfy them. **Why:** COVERAGE marks `io` as design because Reader and Writer are interfaces in Go; everything that streams (bufio over any reader, gzip, tar, zip, streaming hashes, HTTP bodies, multipart) is written against these shapes (design_foundations section 9, step 4). **How:** static dispatch through `[R Reader]` type parameters by default, `dyn Reader` where a heterogeneous list is needed (MultiReader); `io.EOF` becomes a sentinel fault (today `wire.IsEOF`); the buffers come from the caller's region, so `Copy` allocates one buffer per call or uses a caller-supplied one. **Needs:** shapes; fault sentinels. **Done when:** `io.Copy` between a file, a `wire.Conn` and a `bufio`-style writer works in tests, a Go twin in `bench/ref` produces identical output for every ported function including short reads and EOF handling, and `Copy` of 1 GB allocates a constant amount.
- [ ] Atomics for cross-core counters and flags (no mutexes)
  **Work:** a public `atomic` package with the cell types `I64`, `U64` and `Bool` and their `Load`, `Store`, `Add`, `Swap` and `CompareAndSwap`, and the compiler rule that only these types may be declared as a written `shared var`. **Why:** the runtime already uses `__atomic_*` intrinsics privately (LANGUAGE.md section 18), but user code has no way to keep a process-wide counter or flag; share-nothing leaves exactly this need, and limiting cross-core mutable state to what hardware updates atomically is what makes "no mutexes" enforceable (design_foundations section 6). **How:** expose the intrinsics through generic-free methods on the cell types, define the memory ordering (14.1 memory model), extend the checker to reject any other written `shared var` outside `lib/`. **Needs:** nothing technically (14.3 moves it ahead of tasks); the memory-model note in 14.1. **Done when:** a counter incremented by every core under `hearth.Run` sums exactly, a plain `shared var x i64` written by user code is a compile error naming `atomic.I64`, and the operations compile to single instructions (`ldadd`/`lock xadd`) on both CPUs.

Other language work:
- [ ] Range over functions and iterators (`iter.Seq` equivalent) and the `*Seq` forms in the library
  **Work:** let `for x := range f` iterate a function or an iterator value, and add `Seq`-style forms to the library (`twine.SplitSeq`, `Lines`, `atlas.All`/`Keys`/`Values`, `sift.Values`/`All`/`Collect`/`Sorted`). **Why:** COVERAGE lists `iter` as missing and notes that `twine.Lines` returns a slice and `atlas` has no iterator forms; iterators avoid materializing a whole slice in the request pool, which matters when the pool only resets at the end of the request. **How:** the protocol design is in 12.2 ("Iterators and range over functions"): a compile-time shape with a `next` method, lowered to a `WHILE` loop so there is no closure call per element when the iterator is a concrete type; push-style `func(yield)` iterators need capturing closures. **Needs:** closures, shapes, and the optionals decision (a `next` returning `?T` needs `?T` over numbers). **Done when:** ranging over `twine.SplitSeq` allocates no slice, early `break` and `defer` behave as in Go 1.23, and the `*Seq` functions match Go's output in twin tests.
- [ ] Struct embedding with promotion
  **Work:** allow an embedded field (`type Admin struct { User; level i64 }`) whose fields and methods are promoted to the outer type. **Why:** COVERAGE lists embedding as missing; Go code uses it pervasively for composition, and with shapes it is how a type picks up a method set (an embedded `Writer` makes the outer type satisfy `Writer`). **How:** the checker resolves selectors through embedded fields at depth order with Go's ambiguity rule; layout stays a reference to a struct (the embedded struct is a field holding a reference, or inlined; decide and document which, since Tin structs are references); promoted methods get forwarding stubs only when needed for a `dyn` table. **Needs:** shapes for method-set promotion; otherwise none. **Done when:** promotion, shadowing and ambiguity errors match Go's rules in positive and `_bad.tin` tests, JSON encoding of embedded structs matches Go's flattening once derivation lands, and LANGUAGE.md documents the layout.
- [ ] Method values and method expressions
  **Work:** support `f := p.Move` (a function value bound to its receiver) and `g := Point.Move` (the method as a function taking the receiver first). **Why:** COVERAGE lists both as missing; they are the usual way to pass a method as a callback (`r.Get("/x", srv.handle)`), which today needs a wrapper function. **How:** a method expression is just the method's code address; a method value is a closure capturing the receiver, so it reuses the closure representation and region rules (a method value bound to request memory cannot be stored in a global). `mut` receivers stay part of the function type. **Needs:** closures (for method values). **Done when:** both forms work, including on generic types and `mut` receivers, an escaping method value bound to a request object is a region error, and a test shows `srv.handle` passed to an anvil router.
- [ ] Named results and bare `return`
  **Work:** decide whether Tin accepts Go's named results (`func f() (n i64, err fault)`) and bare `return`, then implement or document the omission. **Why:** LANGUAGE.md section 5 says there are no named results; Go code uses them for documentation and for deferred functions that modify results, but with `!T` results the common `err` result disappears, so the need is smaller. **How:** if accepted, named results become locals initialized to zero values and `return` with no operands returns them; `defer` modifying them needs closures. **Needs:** closures for the defer pattern. **Done when:** the decision is in LANGUAGE.md with the reason, and if accepted, tests cover shadowing, defers that set a named result, and interaction with `!T`.
- [ ] User-declared variadic functions
  **Work:** let user code declare `func sum(xs ...i64) i64` and call it with separate arguments or `xs...`. **Why:** COVERAGE marks variadics partial: only the standard library's formatting functions and C externs are variadic today, and `slices.Insert`/`Concat`-style APIs had to take slices instead (`InsertAll`, `ConcatAll` in sift). **How:** lower a variadic parameter to a slice allocated in the caller's region (or on the stack when it does not escape), keep `f(xs...)` passing the slice itself (Tin slices are references, so document that the callee sees the caller's elements). **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** variadic generic functions work, `sift.Insert(mut s, i, a, b, c)` matches Go's `slices.Insert`, and a non-escaping variadic call allocates nothing in a benchmark.
- [ ] `min` and `max` of any number of arguments, `clear`
  **Work:** extend the `min`/`max` builtins from two arguments of one type to any number (Go 1.21 semantics, including NaN and signed zero rules for floats), and add `clear(m)` for maps and `clear(s)` for slices. **Why:** COVERAGE lists `min`/`max` as partial and `clear` as missing; they are small, common Go builtins. **How:** in `chk_builtin`, fold `min(a, b, c)` into nested comparisons (with `csel`/`fcsel`), apply Go's float rules; `clear` on a map resets count, control bytes and tombstones and on a slice zeroes elements. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** a Go twin over all numeric types, NaN, +0/-0 and strings gives identical output, and `clear` on a large map is O(capacity) with no reallocation.
- [ ] Value arrays `[N]T` (copy semantics) next to the slice form
  **Work:** decide and implement a value array type whose assignment and passing copy the elements, distinct from today's `[N]T`, which is a slice starting with N zeros. **Why:** COVERAGE marks arrays partial ("no value semantics"); Go code relies on arrays as values for fixed-size keys (`[16]u8` UUIDs, `[32]u8` hashes as map keys), small vectors and embedded buffers that cost no allocation. **How:** a new layout (inline storage in structs and frames, copied by the code generator), map key support by value, and an edition-gated change if the spelling `[N]T` changes meaning (14.2 puts editions before this). **Needs:** the editions mechanism; the map-key rules item in 14.2. **Done when:** `[32]u8` works as a map key and as a struct field without allocation, assignment copies, and existing programs either keep working or migrate under an edition with a tool.
- [ ] Full slice expressions `s[a:b:c]`
  **Work:** support the three-index slice that limits capacity, and document it. **Why:** COVERAGE says the full slice expression is not documented; it is how Go code prevents `append` on a sub-slice from overwriting the parent, which matters more in Tin because slices are references and `append` grows the header in place (LANGUAGE.md, "Reference semantics"). **How:** add the parse form, bounds checks `0 <= a <= b <= c <= cap`, and set the new header's capacity; decide whether a sub-slice header is new (it must be, so `append` on it cannot change the parent's length). **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** a Go twin covering bounds panics and append-after-reslice behaviour matches, and LANGUAGE.md section 3 documents the semantics.
- [ ] Labels, `goto`-free labeled `break` and `continue`, `fallthrough` decision
  **Work:** add labeled `break` and `continue` for nested loops and switches, keep `goto` out, and decide whether `fallthrough` exists. **Why:** LANGUAGE.md section 7 says there are no labels; breaking out of an outer loop is common in parsers and searches and today needs flags. **How:** labels attach to `for`/`switch`; lowering already turns loops and switches into `WHILE`, so a label maps to the target loop's exit or continue block; `fallthrough` is either rejected with a diagnostic suggesting a shared case list or implemented as a jump to the next case body. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** labeled break/continue work across nested loops and switches, unknown or unused labels are diagnostics, and the `fallthrough` decision is written in LANGUAGE.md.
- [ ] `init` functions decision and documentation
  **Work:** decide whether packages may declare `func init()` and in what order they run, then implement or document the omission. **Why:** COVERAGE marks `init` partial (package variables initialize in declaration order and a forward reference is a compile error); Go code uses `init` for registration and table setup. In Tin globals are per core, so an `init` would run once per core in `__core_init` or once per process for `shared` state, and the docs must say which. **How:** if accepted, `init` bodies are appended to `__core_init` after the package's global initializers, in import order, with the same check that they reach no later global. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** LANGUAGE.md section 5 states the rule, and tests show the order across two imported packages and on several cores.
- [ ] Generic constraints: named constraints, `cmp.Ordered`, constraints with methods (after shapes), generic type aliases
  **Work:** let constraints be named (`shape Ordered = i64 | ... | str` in the library), require methods in constraints, and allow generic type aliases. **Why:** today a constraint is `any`, `comparable` or an inline union (LANGUAGE.md section 12), so signatures repeat an eleven-way union and `cmp.Ordered` has no Tin name (COVERAGE `cmp` row); method constraints are how generic code calls `String()` or `Less`. **How:** reuse the shape machinery: a named union is a shape with no methods, a method constraint is a shape, checked in `generics.tin` at instantiation; aliases re-parse with bound parameters like generic types. **Needs:** shapes. **Done when:** `sift.Ordered` replaces the unions in `sift`, `cmp.Or` and a constraint with a method compile, and constraint failures report the missing type or method at the instantiation site.
- [ ] Generic methods and higher-kinded helpers decision
  **Work:** decide whether methods may have their own type parameters (Go forbids it) and whether any higher-kinded helper is offered. **Why:** iterator adapters (`seq.Map[U]`) and builder APIs want generic methods; Go's reason to forbid them is interface method sets, which Tin's static shapes do not have in the same way, but `dyn` tables cannot hold a generic method. **How:** if accepted, a generic method instantiates like a generic function with the receiver's type bound, and is excluded from `dyn` tables (diagnostic when a shape requires one). **Needs:** shapes. **Done when:** the decision and its reason are in design_foundations.md, with tests if accepted.
- [ ] Complex numbers decision (`complex128`, `math/cmplx`) or a documented omission
  **Work:** decide whether Tin has `complex64`/`complex128` with `complex`, `real`, `imag` and `math/cmplx`, or omits them. **Why:** COVERAGE lists complex types as missing and `math/cmplx` and `strconv.ParseComplex` depend on the decision; servers rarely need them, signal processing does. **How:** if accepted, a value type of two floats passed in two FP registers (needs value types, like value arrays), with Go's formatting; otherwise a library struct `cmplx.C128` with methods. **Needs:** the value-array/value-type work if built into the language. **Done when:** the decision is in LANGUAGE.md, and either `math/cmplx` passes a Go twin or COVERAGE marks it as a documented omission.
- [ ] `//embed` (compile-time file embedding) and generate hooks
  **Work:** embed files into the executable at compile time (`embed` package: a string, a `[]u8` or an `embed.FS`), and define how code generators are run (`tin generate`). **Why:** COVERAGE lists `embed` and `//go:embed`/`//go:generate` as missing; servers embed templates, static assets and migrations, and a single static binary is one of Tin's selling points (35 KB hello world). **How:** a directive or attribute on a global (`@embed("static/*")`) that the compiler resolves relative to the package, writing the bytes into the constant segment; an `embed.FS` satisfies the `io/fs` shapes; generate hooks are a `tin generate` command reading declared commands, subject to package capabilities. **Needs:** attributes (#145) for the spelling; io/fs shapes for `embed.FS`. **Done when:** a server serves an embedded directory with no file reads at run time, builds stay reproducible, and embedding a missing file is a compile error.
- [ ] `unsafe`-equivalent: a small, audited raw-memory package for the standard library only
  **Work:** gather the raw operations that `lib/` uses today (`cast`, word indexing, `load8`/`store8`, `__ld`/`__st`, `&x`, LANGUAGE.md section 18) into one named, documented package with a short audited surface. **Why:** `unsafe` is design in COVERAGE: user code has no raw memory, and the region checker's guarantees depend on raw access being confined; naming it makes audits and the `unsafe` capability (#146) possible. **How:** move the intrinsics behind a package (`raw` or similar) that only `lib/` and packages granted the `unsafe` capability may import; each use site is greppable; region effects of each operation are written down. **Needs:** packages with capabilities for the non-stdlib grant. **Done when:** every raw operation in `lib/` goes through the package, a user import without the capability is a compile error, and the package's rules are in LANGUAGE.md section 18.
- [x] Integer overflow policy (wrapping vs checked, per type) written down and tested (#362: checked by default in user code and libraries, `+% -% *%` and `@wrap` to wrap; notes/design_foundations.md section 11)
  **Work:** decide the overflow rule per type and context (today all integer arithmetic wraps, LANGUAGE.md sections 6 and 17) and whether a checked mode or checked operators exist. **Why:** wrapping silently is a common source of security bugs (lengths, sizes); a checked debug mode or explicit `checked`/`wrapping` operations make intent visible, in line with "checked at compile time" where possible. **How:** options to decide between: wrap everywhere (Go), trap in debug builds only, or explicit operator families; constant overflow is already a compile error (`adapt_int`). Changing the default is breaking, so it goes through editions (14.2). **Needs:** editions if the default changes. **Done when:** LANGUAGE.md states the rule, tests cover every width and operator at the boundaries, and the chosen debug behaviour is exercised in CI.
- [ ] Optionals: decide whether `?T` extends to number, bool and enum types (today `?T` is for reference types) and write the rule; binding sugar decision
  **Work:** decide whether `?i64`, `?bool` and `?Color` exist (which need a separate presence flag, since 0 is a valid value) and whether binding sugar such as `if v := m.Get(k)?` is added. **Why:** LANGUAGE.md section 9 limits `?T` to reference types, which blocks iterators returning `?T` for numbers, nullable database columns and `json` optional numbers; the decision affects 12.2 (iterator protocol) and database scanning. **How:** a non-reference optional is a two-word value (value plus flag) returned in two registers; narrowing works as today. **Needs:** nothing, but iterators and `sql.Null*` wait on it. **Done when:** the rule is in LANGUAGE.md with the representation, and if accepted, narrowing tests cover every scalar kind and JSON `null` decodes into `?i64`.
- [ ] Pattern matching: nested patterns, guards, `switch` on tuples
  **Work:** extend enum `switch` with nested patterns (`case Named(_, Circle(r))`), guards (`case Rect(w, h) if w == h`), literal patterns and switching on several values at once. **Why:** enums with exhaustive switch replace interfaces for closed sets (design_foundations section 2), so their ergonomics carry much of the language; today a case binds one level only (LANGUAGE.md, "Enums"). **How:** compile patterns to decision trees in `check.tin` and keep the exhaustiveness checker sound (a guarded case does not count toward exhaustiveness). **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** nested and guarded patterns work, exhaustiveness errors name the missing nested variant, and the generated code is no slower than hand-written nested switches.
- [ ] Const evaluation: compile-time functions, typed const generics
  **Work:** allow calling simple pure functions in constant expressions and decide on const generic parameters (`[N const i64]`). **Why:** today only literal expressions fold (`fold_const`); tables (CRC, Unicode, lookup tables) are generated by Python scripts (`tools/gen_unicode.py`) or written by hand, and fixed-size algorithms want sizes as parameters. **How:** an interpreter over the lowered tree for a restricted subset (no allocation escaping, no I/O), with a step limit; const generic parameters instantiate like type parameters. **Needs:** value arrays for const-sized types. **Done when:** a CRC table computed at compile time is byte-identical to the generated one, a step-limit overrun is a clear diagnostic, and compile time does not regress on the compiler's own build.
- [ ] Formal grammar and a language specification document, versioned
  **Work:** turn LANGUAGE.md's reference and EBNF (section 19) into a versioned specification with precise semantics for every construct. **Why:** a second implementation, tooling (formatter, LSP, tree-sitter) and the compatibility promise all need an authoritative text; today the compiler is the specification. **How:** start from the grammar in section 19, add typing, evaluation order, region rules and runtime behaviour; every example in the spec is a test run by the suite (14.6). **Needs:** the foundations settled (closures, shapes, faults, tasks) so the text is not rewritten. **Done when:** a versioned spec exists in docs, every grammar rule is exercised by the parser tests, and spec examples run in CI.
- [ ] Compatibility promise and edition mechanism (breaking changes only by edition)
  **Work:** define what may change between releases and add editions: a per-package declaration that selects language rules, so old and new code link together. **Why:** value arrays, the overflow policy and syntax cleanups are breaking; without editions they either never happen or break every program; 14.2 and 14.3 move this to year 1 because the registry and third-party code make breaks expensive. **How:** an `edition` field in the package manifest read by the parser and checker, per-file rule switches, and a migration tool that rewrites code between editions. **Needs:** packages (#146) for the manifest. **Done when:** two packages on different editions build into one program, a rule that differs by edition is tested both ways, and the promise is published in docs.

### 2. Compiler (year 1 to 5)

The compiler is `selfhost/` (about 17,000 lines of legacy-syntax Tin, docs/COMPILER.md). Every item keeps the invariant that `make bootstrap` reaches a byte-identical fixed point.

Correctness:
- [ ] A conformance suite: Tin's own spec tests, and the corpus of Go programs ported as differential tests
  **Work:** a suite organized by specification section, plus Go programs ported to Tin whose output must match the Go original. **Why:** today correctness rests on `tests/v2` (145 files, output compared with `.out`) and the stdlib twins in `bench/ref`; a spec-indexed suite shows which rules are covered and catches regressions a feature-oriented suite misses. **How:** one directory per spec section with positive tests and `_bad.tin`/`.err` negatives, run by the existing `tools/v2test.sh` runner; differential programs live next to their Go twin like `bench/v2`. **Needs:** the specification document (section 1) for the index. **Done when:** every spec section has tests, the suite runs on all three targets in CI, and a coverage report lists untested rules.
- [ ] Differential fuzzing of the compiler against the interpreter-free reference outputs (Go twins)
  **Work:** generate random programs in the subset Tin and Go share, compile both, and compare outputs. **Why:** miscompiles hide in combinations hand-written tests never try; Go is a reliable oracle for the shared subset (integer wrapping, float printing, string and map behaviour). **How:** a generator over a restricted grammar (14.5 asks for the grammar subset to be listed) emits a Tin file and a Go file from one description, as `tests/v2/bits.tin` already does for `bench/ref/bits`; mismatches are reduced automatically (14.6). **Needs:** a reducer for usable reports. **Done when:** the fuzzer runs nightly, has found and regression-tested its first bugs, and the generated subset is documented.
- [ ] Fuzzing the lexer, parser and checker (no crash on any input, errors with positions)
  **Work:** feed random and mutated source to the front end and require a diagnostic with a position, never a crash or hang. **Why:** COMPILER.md lists crash modes (a node rewritten twice, an unresolved `ID_REF` crashing `analyze_fn`); a compiler crash gives the user nothing and AI-generated code will hit odd inputs. **How:** mutate the `tests/v2` corpus (token deletion, duplication, splicing), run `tinc` with a timeout, and treat a signal or a missing `file:line:col` as a failure; crashing inputs become `_bad.tin` regression cases. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** a million mutated inputs run without a crash or hang in CI's nightly job and every found crash has a regression case.
- [ ] LLVM-style test coverage: every pass has lit-style tests for what it must and must not do
  **Work:** per-pass tests that check the transformed code (assembly via `tinc -S`, or a pass dump) contains or lacks specific patterns. **Why:** output-only tests cannot tell whether `licm_fn` hoisted, the inliner inlined or a bounds check was removed, so optimizations regress silently. **How:** a test file holds source plus `CHECK:`/`CHECK-NOT:` lines matched against `-S` output; extend the existing runner rather than adding a new tool. **Needs:** stable assembly output (already printed by `asm.tin`/`asm_x64.tin`). **Done when:** every pass in COMPILER.md section 8 and the codegen optimizations in section 7 have at least one positive and one negative check on each CPU.
- [ ] Error messages: every diagnostic has a code, a span, a suggestion where one exists
  **Work:** give each diagnostic a stable code (`E0123`), a start and end position, and a fix-it where the fix is known. **Why:** errors print as `file:line:col: error: message` today (TOOLING.md section 3); codes make errors searchable and documentable (14.5 asks for a page per code), spans let editors underline, and suggestions matter for a language meant to be written by AI and humans alike. **How:** route every `err_begin` call through a table of codes; carry end positions from the lexer; keep the existing `.err` tests and add the code to them. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** no diagnostic lacks a code, the checklist of error classes that must carry a fix-it (14.5) is complete, and the LSP shows spans.
- [ ] Compile-time region checker proofs for the documented escape rules; counterexample corpus
  **Work:** a written argument (and later a mechanized one, 14.4) that the rules in `region.tin` prevent request memory from being reachable from long-lived memory, plus a corpus of programs that try to break them. **Why:** the region checker replaces a garbage collector; a hole is a use-after-reset, i.e. memory unsafety, so its rules need more than tests. **How:** state the abstract rules from COMPILER.md section 6 (region bits, holds, summaries), argue soundness per rule, and keep every attempted escape (globals, closures, `mut` function values, containers holding globals) as a `_bad.tin` test. **Needs:** closures and tasks change the rules, so the proof is revisited after each. **Done when:** the document covers every store form, the counterexample corpus has a case per rule, and the region fuzzer (14.6) finds nothing.
- [ ] Reproducible builds: the same source gives the same bytes on every machine
  **Work:** guarantee byte-identical output across machines, paths and times. **Why:** `make bootstrap` already proves self-consistency on one host and the Mach-O UUID is a hash of the code (COMPILER.md section 9), but supply-chain claims (14.6 bootstrap provenance, signed releases) need cross-machine reproducibility. **How:** audit for embedded absolute paths, timestamps, hash-map iteration order in the compiler and host-dependent defaults; build the same commit on two CI machines per target and compare. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** CI builds each target on two runners and the outputs are identical, including the cross-compiled ones.

Performance of the generated code:
- [ ] Inliner for multi-statement functions (the cause of the remaining math and sort gaps)
  **Work:** inline functions with several statements, not only `return expr` bodies of up to 40 nodes (`inline_small_calls`). **Why:** PERFORMANCE.md sections 3b and 3c attribute gauge's 1.2 to 1.8x gap and generic `sift.Sort`'s 1.28x gap against Go to calls Go inlines (`IsNaN`, `Copysign`, comparators); this is the single highest-payoff codegen item. **How:** detailed tasks in 12.4: a size and call-count cost model, inlining across packages after monomorphization, renaming locals, mapping `return` to jumps, preserving `mut` receivers and frame-pointer backtraces. **Needs:** nothing, though an SSA middle end would simplify it. **Done when:** generic `sift.Sort` on i64 is within 5 percent of `sift.Ints`, gauge's sin/cos/log are within 1.2x of Go, and no benchmark regresses.
- [ ] Intrinsics: clz, ctz, popcount, rbit, rev, fma, sqrt, rounding, multiply-high, add-with-carry
  **Work:** compile the `bits` and `gauge` functions that have one-instruction forms to that instruction on both CPUs. **Why:** `bits` is verified against Go but written in portable Tin; float rounding and sqrt are already instructions (COMPILER.md section 8), the integer ones are not; division by constants via multiply-high is on PERFORMANCE.md's list, and TLS needs carry-less multiply (14.3). **How:** recognize the library functions by name in `inline.tin` as the float intrinsics are, emit `clz`/`rbit`/`cnt`/`rev`/`umulh`/`adcs` on arm64 and `lzcnt`/`tzcnt`/`popcnt`/`bswap`/`mul`/`adc` on amd64 with fallbacks when the CPU lacks them; FMA must be explicit only (to keep gauge's bit-for-bit corpus results stable). **Needs:** CPU feature detection for amd64 (12.4). **Done when:** each function's generated code is the single instruction (lit-style check), `bench/ref/bits` stays identical, and `% 10` uses multiply-high.
- [ ] Constant hoisting and strength reduction; loop-invariant code motion
  **Work:** hoist 64-bit constant materialization (`movz`/`movk` sequences) out of loops and functions, and extend strength reduction and LICM. **Why:** PERFORMANCE.md section 3 lists constants rebuilt inside loops as a cause of the n-body, fannkuch and math gaps; a six-term polynomial rebuilds a dozen coefficients per call. **How:** `licm_fn` already hoists invariant expressions; add constants as hoistable values with a register-pressure check, or load them from a literal pool; extend shift-and-add strength reduction to induction variables. **Needs:** better register allocation to hold hoisted values. **Done when:** gauge's polynomials load constants once per call or from a pool (lit-style check) and math benchmarks improve measurably.
- [ ] Bounds-check elimination from range and induction facts
  **Work:** remove bounds checks proven redundant by loop facts beyond today's cases (range loops, `i < len(s)` loops, `if i < len(s)`; LANGUAGE.md section 17). **Why:** PERFORMANCE.md names checks the prover cannot remove (`j < n` where `n == len(s)` is known only through another variable) as a cause of the fannkuch gap. **How:** track equalities between locals and lengths, monotonic induction variables and dominating checks; in the SSA middle end this becomes a range analysis. **Needs:** an SSA middle end for the general form. **Done when:** the fannkuch and n-body inner loops have no checks (lit-style), and a negative test shows a check is kept when the length can change.
- [ ] Register allocation: linear scan to a graph or SSA-based allocator
  **Work:** replace today's homes (callee-saved x19–x27 and d8–d15 chosen per function by loop-weighted use counts, plus a depth-indexed temporary stack) with a real allocator. **Why:** PERFORMANCE.md section 3: in large loops whole-function allocation runs out of registers and loop variables live in stack slots (fannkuch, n-body). **How:** live ranges per value, loop-depth spill weights, caller-saved registers for values not live across calls, then a linear-scan or graph-colouring allocator on SSA; tested on the whole corpus (12.4). **Needs:** an SSA middle end, or at least liveness. **Done when:** fannkuch and n-body are at or below Go's times and the self-build stays a fixed point.
- [ ] An SSA middle end (or equivalent) with common subexpression elimination and dead store elimination
  **Work:** introduce an SSA intermediate form between lowering and codegen, with a verifier, and move optimizations onto it. **Why:** the current pipeline lowers the AST in place and generates code from the tree (COMPILER.md section 2), which makes data-flow optimizations (CSE, DSE, alias information for struct fields, range analysis) hard; PERFORMANCE.md's alias problem (stores through one struct invalidate loads of another) needs it. **How:** detailed in 12.4 and split in 14.4: build SSA from lowered trees, verify, add passes one at a time behind flags with the whole corpus as the test. **Needs:** constant-time codegen rules decided first (14.2) so crypto code is not broken by the optimizer. **Done when:** both backends generate from SSA, `make bootstrap` is a fixed point, and the bench/v2 suite improves on the geometric mean.
- [ ] Escape and region analysis that stack-allocates request-local values
  **Work:** allocate values that never escape their function in the frame instead of the request pool. **Why:** a pool allocation is cheap (a bump) but its memory lives until the request ends; stack allocation keeps long requests and plain programs bounded (PERFORMANCE.md notes binary-trees uses 917 MB against Go's 37 MB because a plain program never resets its pool). **How:** reuse the region summaries in `region.tin`: a fresh allocation not stored, returned or passed to a sink parameter can live in the frame; non-escaping closure cells already plan this (design_foundations section 1). **Needs:** closures (shares the analysis). **Done when:** a loop allocating a temporary struct per iteration uses constant memory, binary-trees' resident size drops, and no region test regresses.
- [ ] SIMD: vector types, auto-vectorization of simple loops, hand-written kernels for memchr, memcmp, hashing, base64, utf8
  **Work:** vector types in the language (12.4), auto-vectorization of simple counted loops, and NEON/AVX2 kernels for the byte-processing hot paths. **Why:** anvil already relies on `memchr` from libc for header scanning and argo uses 8-byte SWAR (RUNTIME.md section 10); removing libc (section 3) means Tin needs its own fast kernels, and parsing-heavy services spend their time in exactly these loops. **How:** first hand-written kernels behind the standard library functions, selected by runtime CPU detection; then vector types with lane-width checks; then loop vectorization on SSA. **Needs:** CPU feature detection; SSA for auto-vectorization. **Done when:** memchr, memcmp, utf8 validation and base64 are at least as fast as libc/Go on 1 KB and 1 MB inputs on both CPUs, with identical results.
- [ ] Profile-guided optimization (inlining and layout from a recorded profile)
  **Work:** read a CPU profile (the pprof format of section 3) and use it for inlining decisions, hot/cold block layout and function ordering. **Why:** Go has PGO since 1.21 with 2 to 14 percent gains; for Tin it is the way to make inlining decisions that a static cost model gets wrong. **How:** map profile samples to functions and blocks via the symbol and line tables, weight the inliner's cost model, place cold stubs (already separate) and cold blocks out of line. **Needs:** the profiler and DWARF line tables; the inliner. **Done when:** a recorded profile of the HTTP benchmark improves it measurably, and builds with a profile stay reproducible.
- [ ] Link-time optimization across packages; dead data and code stripping
  **Work:** optimize across package boundaries and remove unreachable code and data. **Why:** the compiler already sees the whole program and marks reachable functions (COMPILER.md section 2), so cross-package inlining is natural; data (Unicode tables, unused constants) is not yet stripped, which matters for the binary-size budget. **How:** extend reachability to globals and constant data, run the inliner after monomorphization across packages (12.4). **Needs:** the inliner. **Done when:** a program that imports `glyph` but uses one function does not carry the unused tables, and the binary-size ceilings of 14.5 hold.
- [ ] Monomorphization cost control: shared instantiation for identical machine code
  **Work:** emit one copy of a generic instantiation when several type arguments produce identical machine code (for example any reference type, since every reference is one word). **Why:** monomorphization re-parses and compiles each instantiation (COMPILER.md section 5), so code size and compile time grow with the number of types; shapes and derivation will multiply instantiations. **How:** hash the generated code per instantiation and fold duplicates at link time, or instantiate per layout class (all reference types share one) when the body does not depend on the type beyond its layout. **Needs:** nothing; 11 keeps dictionary passing as an open question. **Done when:** the compiler and the standard library tests show fewer emitted functions and smaller binaries with no runtime change.
- [ ] Compile speed: incremental and parallel builds, a build cache keyed by content
  **Work:** cache per-package results keyed by content hash and check packages in parallel. **Why:** the compiler builds itself in 0.07 s warm (PERFORMANCE.md section 4), so this matters once programs and dependency trees grow; 12.4 sets `tin run` under a second for small programs. **How:** detailed in 12.4 ("Build speed"): parallel parse and check, a per-package object cache, incremental relink. Whole-program reachability and monomorphization complicate per-package caching, so the cache key includes the instantiations a package needs. **Needs:** packages (#146) for package identity. **Done when:** a one-line change in a large program rebuilds faster than a clean build by a stated factor and outputs are identical to a clean build.
- [ ] Debug info: DWARF line tables and variables, so debuggers and profilers work
  **Work:** emit DWARF (and the Mach-O equivalent) with line tables, then variable locations and types. **Why:** today `lldb` sees function names only, panics name frames through `dladdr` and inlined frames are missing (TOOLING.md section 8); profilers need line attribution; 14.3 moves line tables to years 1 to 2 because the first production service needs them. **How:** record positions (already packed in tokens and nodes) through lowering into the instruction list, emit `.debug_line` in `elf.tin`/`elf_x64.tin` and the Mach-O `__DWARF` segment, then locations for locals' homes. **Needs:** nothing for line tables. **Done when:** `lldb` and `gdb` break on a source line and step on all three targets, `perf`/Instruments attribute samples to lines, and builds stay reproducible.

Targets:
- [ ] linux-arm64, linux-amd64, darwin-arm64 at full parity (done for the first three: keep green)
  **Work:** keep the three supported targets passing every suite and self-hosting. **Why:** CI runs all three natively and the Linux port is done (roadmap header); every new feature must land on both backends (`gen.tin`, `gen_x64.tin`) at once or the targets drift. **How:** the CI gate already requires bootstrap fixed points and all suites per target (docs/CI.md); the 12.1 template requires codegen on arm64 and amd64 for every feature. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** this stays checked only as long as every release passes all suites on all three targets; it is a standing gate rather than a one-time task.
- [ ] darwin-amd64
  **Work:** support Intel Macs: Mach-O output with the x86-64 backend. **Why:** the x86-64 backend exists for Linux and the Mach-O writer exists for arm64, so this target is mostly the combination; Intel Macs are still in use by developers. **How:** teach `macho.tin` x86-64 relocations, stubs and the CPU type, reuse `gen_x64.tin`, and port the darwin runtime pieces that differ by CPU (task switch `rt_task_swap` already exists for x86-64). **Needs:** a macOS x86-64 CI runner. **Done when:** darwin-amd64 bootstraps to a fixed point and passes every suite on a native runner.
- [ ] Windows (amd64, arm64): PE writer, Win32 runtime part, IOCP
  **Work:** a Windows target: PE/COFF writer, a Win32 runtime part, and IOCP-based I/O. **Why:** a language "as ready as Go" for tools must build Windows binaries; 14.4 lists the parts as separate tasks (PE writer, structured exception handling and unwinding, Win32 runtime, IOCP on a completion-capable layer, path and console semantics, a Windows CI runner). **How:** follow 14.4's split; IOCP is completion-based, so the completion-capable I/O layer of 14.2 comes first; the FFI policy decides how kernel32 is called. **Needs:** FFI policy, the completion-capable I/O layer, unwinding for `guard`. **Done when:** Windows amd64 passes the strict suite and the HTTP conformance tests on a Windows CI runner, then arm64.
- [ ] FreeBSD and OpenBSD (kqueue is shared with darwin)
  **Work:** ELF targets for FreeBSD and OpenBSD on amd64 and arm64. **Why:** the event loop's kqueue code already exists for macOS (`anvil_darwin.tin`), so the BSDs mainly need their syscall ABIs and struct layouts; they are common for network appliances. **How:** add `*_freebsd.tin`/`*_openbsd.tin` runtime files with the OS layer helpers of RUNTIME.md section 8 and verified constants (as `notes/linux_abi.md` does for Linux); OpenBSD requires syscalls through libc (pinsyscalls), which the FFI and no-libc policies must allow. **Needs:** the libc policy decisions in section 3 and 14.2. **Done when:** each BSD passes the strict suite and HTTP conformance in CI (a VM job).
- [ ] riscv64
  **Work:** a third CPU backend for RISC-V 64-bit (RV64GC) on Linux. **Why:** RISC-V servers and boards are growing; a third backend also tests that the compiler's CPU-specific parts are well separated. **How:** an instruction list, encoder and printer like `asm.tin`, a code generator modelled on `gen.tin`, the task switch in assembly, ELF relocations; fuzz the encoder against objdump as `tools/x64fuzz` does. **Needs:** ideally the SSA middle end first, so the third backend does not triple tree-walking codegen. **Done when:** linux-riscv64 bootstraps to a fixed point under QEMU or native hardware and passes the strict suite.
- [ ] WebAssembly (wasm32-wasi first, then browser); needs its own design note first: stackful tasks need stack switching or asyncify, and there are no threads-per-core (see 14.4)
  **Work:** a wasm32 backend, starting with WASI and then the browser (for the playground). **Why:** a browser playground (section 5) and edge runtimes need wasm; but Tin's runtime model (stackful tasks, one thread per core, `rt_task_swap`) does not map directly. **How:** write the design note first (14.4): one core, stack switching via the wasm stack-switching proposal or an asyncify transform, files and sockets through WASI, a size budget; then a backend emitting wasm bytecode from the lowered tree or SSA. **Needs:** the design note; SSA would help (wasm is structured). **Done when:** the strict suite (minus thread tests) passes under a WASI runtime and the playground compiles and runs a program in the browser.
- [ ] Embedded and freestanding targets (no OS runtime part)
  **Work:** a freestanding mode with no OS layer: no files, sockets or threads, a user-provided allocator and entry point. **Why:** after libc removal the runtime's OS dependence is concentrated in the OS layer (RUNTIME.md section 8), so a freestanding target is the runtime minus that layer; useful for kernels, bootloaders and microcontrollers. **How:** a `freestanding` target that omits the OS files, makes the request pool a static arena, and turns panics into a user hook. **Needs:** libc removal; the allocator rework. **Done when:** a freestanding program runs under QEMU on arm64 bare metal and prints over a UART hook.
- [ ] A second backend (LLVM IR emitter) as an optimization-quality reference, not a dependency
  **Work:** an optional backend that emits LLVM IR text, used to compare code quality, never required to build Tin. **Why:** it shows how far Tin's own optimizer is from a mature one on each benchmark, which guides the performance programme; Tin must not depend on LLVM (no external toolchain is involved today). **How:** emit textual IR from SSA, compile it with a locally installed clang in a benchmark job only. **Needs:** the SSA middle end. **Done when:** the bench/v2 suite builds through the LLVM path with identical output and a report compares times per benchmark.

### 3. Runtime (year 1 to 5)

The runtime is `lib/runtime/` plus the server packages built on it (docs/RUNTIME.md). Its fixed points are one thread per core, share-nothing, request pools reset per request, and tasks that switch only where they park.

- [ ] Allocator: size classes, per-core caches, huge-page support, no libc (libc removal phases 2 to 6, #125)
  **Work:** finish the allocator so it takes memory straight from the kernel (`mmap`) instead of `calloc`/`malloc`, keeps per-core caches, and can back pools and slabs with huge pages. **Why:** today the request pool takes 4 MiB chunks, blocks of 256 KiB or more are calloc'd, the ingot heap carves 1 MiB slabs and sends big blocks to calloc, and relay nodes are malloc'd (RUNTIME.md sections 3 and 5); libc's allocator has global locks and is the main reason Linux binaries need glibc 2.34+ (DISTRIBUTION.md). **How:** follow #125's phases: an mmap-backed page source per core, size-class slabs for the ingot heap (the 16 classes exist), big blocks as their own mappings returned with `munmap`, transparent or explicit huge pages for pool chunks, and a cross-core free path that sends a block back to its owning core (blocks never cross cores today). **Needs:** the raw-syscall layer (next item) on Linux. **Done when:** no Tin program on Linux imports `malloc`, `calloc` or `free`, the HTTP benchmark and the 200-cycle pool reset test show no regression, and RSS stays stable over two million requests as the CI check already requires.
- [ ] Linux without libc: raw syscalls everywhere, vDSO clock
  **Work:** replace every libc call on Linux with a raw system call, read the clock through the vDSO, and start programs at `_start` without `__libc_start_main`. **Why:** Linux binaries currently link glibc through `PT_INTERP` and call `__libc_start_main` (COMPILER.md section 9), so they cannot run on Alpine/musl or scratch images, and libc adds startup cost and size; the RUNTIME.md OS layer is already one file per OS, so the change is contained. **How:** a syscall intrinsic per CPU (`svc #0` / `syscall`), the OS layer helpers (`rt_errno`, `rt_mono_ns`, `rt_random`, sockets, stat, dirent) reimplemented on it, a static ELF with no interpreter, the vDSO located through the auxiliary vector for `clock_gettime`, threads created with `clone` instead of pthreads; DNS, number formatting and the allocator are separate items. **Needs:** the allocator, number formatting and DNS items below. **Done when:** `readelf` shows no `PT_INTERP` and no dynamic imports for a Linux Tin binary, every suite passes in an empty (scratch) container on arm64 and amd64, and hello world starts faster than today.
- [ ] Number parsing and printing without libc (strtod, snprintf replacements)
  **Work:** shortest float formatting and correctly rounded parsing written in Tin. **Why:** float printing tries `snprintf("%.*e")` at increasing precision and checks with `strtod` when the fast path does not apply (RUNTIME.md section 6), which is slow and depends on libc; `mint.ParseFloat` and argo's float reader must be exact. **How:** port a shortest-round-trip algorithm (Ryu or Go's `strconv` approach, which mint already mirrors) and Eisel-Lemire parsing with a big-decimal fallback, used by `say`, `argo` and `mint`. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** a corpus of several million doubles (edge cases, subnormals, random bits) formats and parses bit-identically to Go's `strconv`, and JSON encoding of floats gets faster.
- [ ] DNS resolver in Tin (stub resolver, /etc/hosts, search domains, happy eyeballs)
  **Work:** a non-blocking DNS stub resolver on the core's event loop, reading `/etc/hosts` and `/etc/resolv.conf`, with search domains, A/AAAA queries and happy-eyeballs connection racing. **Why:** name resolution today calls `getaddrinfo` on the four shared helper threads (RUNTIME.md, "Non-blocking I/O"), which ties it to libc and lets slow DNS fill the 4096-job helper queue; a resolver on the event loop parks only the requesting task. **How:** UDP sockets (needs UDP in `wire`), TCP fallback for truncated answers, a per-core cache respecting TTLs, the ambient deadline on every query; happy eyeballs uses a scope with two child tasks. **Needs:** UDP in `net`, tasks and scopes for racing. **Done when:** resolution of names from `/etc/hosts` and a test DNS server (with truncation, NXDOMAIN, timeouts and search lists) matches Go's pure resolver, and a stalled DNS server no longer delays unrelated requests.
- [ ] io_uring backend next to epoll and kqueue
  **Work:** an io_uring event backend on Linux, optional at run time, alongside epoll. **Why:** io_uring removes a system call per read/write and gives truly asynchronous file I/O, which would let `quarry` stop using helper threads for files; but it is completion-based while the current loops are readiness-based (14.2). **How:** design the completion-capable I/O layer first (14.2), then implement submission and completion rings per core, with fixed buffers from the core's pool, falling back to epoll where io_uring is disabled (many container runtimes block it). **Needs:** the completion-capable I/O layer; raw syscalls. **Done when:** every suite passes with the io_uring backend forced on, file reads no longer use helper threads under it, and the HTTP benchmark is no slower than epoll.
- [ ] Task scheduler: request placement across cores at accept time (least loaded core), never migration of a running task (a task shares its parent's pool, so moving it would move a pool across cores); fairness by round-robin within a core and priority by deadline; acceptance: a 100 ms handler never delays a fast one on its core (wrk2 mix), p99 within 10 percent of the single-class run
  **Work:** formalize the scheduler: placement of new connections on the least-loaded core at accept time (Linux already hands a new connection to a less loaded core using per-core counters, RUNTIME.md section 9), round-robin fairness among ready tasks on a core, and deadline priority (a task closer to its deadline runs first). **Why:** tasks never migrate (no work stealing across cores) because a task's region lives in its core's pool; so the only balancing point is accept time, and the only lever inside a core is ordering. **How:** extend the per-core ready queue into a deadline-ordered structure with a round-robin tie-break; apply the same least-loaded placement on macOS, where core 0 deals connections round-robin today; expose counters for the watchdog and observability. **Needs:** nothing new; tasks and scopes add more tasks per core to schedule. **Done when:** the wrk2 slow/fast mix shows the fast class's p99 within 10 percent of a run with only fast requests, on Linux and macOS.
- [ ] A watchdog that reports (and optionally kills the request of) a task that never parks within a budget; no preemption, because tasks switch only where they park and that is why there are no mutexes
  **Work:** detect a task that runs longer than a budget without parking and report it with its backtrace, optionally failing its request. **Why:** cooperative scheduling means a CPU-bound handler stalls every other request on its core; preemption would break the "no race on a core" guarantee that removes mutexes, so the answer is detection plus the explicit polling point `task.Canceled()` (design_foundations section 4). **How:** a per-core "last park" timestamp updated in `rt_task_swap`, checked by a monitor thread or a timer signal; reporting walks the stalled thread's frame pointers; "kill" sets the task's cancel flag so its next poll or wait fails, never interrupting it mid-instruction. **Needs:** cancellation (#144) for the kill option. **Done when:** a test handler that spins for 500 ms with a 100 ms budget is reported with a symbolized backtrace, and with the kill option its next `task.Canceled()` check fails the request with 503 while other requests continue.
- [ ] Task stacks: large lazily committed reservations with guard pages (no copying: non-escaping closure cells point into the stack); acceptance: 100,000 parked tasks on one core within a stated memory budget
  **Work:** reserve larger virtual stacks per task and commit pages only when touched, keeping the guard region. **Why:** each task has a 256 KiB mmap'd stack with a 16 KiB guard (RUNTIME.md, "Request tasks"), which limits deep recursion (argo caps nesting at 512 for this reason) and costs memory per parked task; Go-style stack copying is ruled out because non-escaping closure cells and frame-local values are addressed directly. **How:** reserve for example 8 MiB per task with `PROT_NONE`, commit on fault or with `MAP_NORESERVE`, return idle stacks' pages with `madvise(DONTNEED)` when tasks go to the free list; tune the reservation per core count. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** 100,000 parked WebSocket-style tasks fit on one core within a stated RSS budget, a deep recursion test passes that fails today, and the fast path's two switches stay at about 10 ns.
- [ ] Timers: hierarchical wheel, monotonic clocks, timer slack
  **Work:** replace the per-core min-heap of sleeping tasks with a hierarchical timer wheel, keep everything on the monotonic clock, and allow timer slack to batch wake-ups. **Why:** every wait pushes a timer for its timeout or deadline (RUNTIME.md, "Non-blocking I/O"), and with 100,000 tasks and frequent cancels a heap's O(log n) insert/remove and stale-entry skipping add up; `tide`'s Timer, Ticker and After (12.3) will add more timers. **How:** a wheel with millisecond resolution at the first level, cascading levels for longer timeouts, O(1) cancel by generation number (as today), and the event loop waiting until the next slot. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** a benchmark with 100,000 timers armed and cancelled per second costs less CPU than the heap, and the request-task CI checks still pass.
- [ ] Panics: backtraces with symbolized frames in release builds, core dumps, crash reports
  **Work:** symbolize panic backtraces without `dladdr`, include inlined frames and line numbers, optionally write a core dump, and produce a structured crash report. **Why:** `rt_panic` names frames with `dladdr` and the Linux ELF exports every function as `tin.<name>` just for that (RUNTIME.md section 7), which depends on libc and misses inlined frames; production services need file:line and a report a tool can collect. **How:** embed a compact function and line table (from the DWARF work) read by the runtime itself; on panic print `pkg.Func file:line` per frame; core dumps via `setrlimit` and the default signal action when enabled; a JSON crash report on stderr when an environment variable asks. **Needs:** DWARF line tables (section 2); libc removal drops `dladdr`. **Done when:** a panic in a release build prints file and line for every frame including inlined ones on all targets, and a CI test checks the format.
- [ ] Memory limits per request, per core and per process, with backpressure
  **Work:** enforce memory budgets at three levels: a request whose pool exceeds its budget fails, a core over budget stops accepting, and the process stays under a limit. **Why:** a single request can grow its pool without bound today (only bodies are capped at 64 MiB and in-flight requests at 4096 per core); in containers the OOM killer takes the whole process, so Tin should fail one request instead. `hearth.MemLimit` exists and the guard design leaves a per-request quota open (design_foundations section 10). **How:** count pool chunks and big blocks per task (they are already tracked for reset), fail the allocation with a fault-carrying panic caught by `guard`, shed load at accept time when a core is over budget, and read the cgroup memory limit at start as `hearth.Cores()` reads the CPU quota. **Needs:** `guard` for turning an over-budget request into a 503. **Done when:** a handler that allocates without bound gets a 503 while other requests continue, and the process stays under its cgroup limit in a CI test.
- [ ] Observability built in: counters, histograms, trace spans, the pprof format
  **Work:** runtime-provided metrics (per-core counters and latency histograms), trace spans, and profile output in the pprof format. **Why:** COVERAGE's "performance tooling" list (`runtime/pprof`, `net/http/pprof`, `runtime/metrics`) exists because the end goal is performance and it cannot be improved without measurement; services also need request metrics without a third-party agent. **How:** per-core counters and histograms updated without atomics (each core owns its cells) and summed on read through `relay` or atomics; a sampling CPU profiler using a timer signal and frame-pointer walks (frame pointers are always kept); heap profiles as pool and ingot usage per allocation site; output as pprof protobuf. 14.5 asks for the list of counters and span names. **Needs:** DWARF/line tables for useful profiles; atomics. **Done when:** `go tool pprof` (or `tin pprof`) opens a Tin CPU profile with correct function and line attribution, and anvil exposes request counters and latency histograms with tests.
- [ ] Signals, process control, fork-free spawn, pipes, sockets options, `sendfile`, `splice`
  **Work:** a public signal API, process spawning without `fork` (posix_spawn or `clone(CLONE_VFORK)`), pipes, the common socket options, and zero-copy `sendfile`/`splice`. **Why:** anvil handles SIGTERM/SIGINT internally but user code cannot (COVERAGE `os/signal`), `os/exec` is missing, and serving static files without copying through user space is a standard server optimization. **How:** signals delivered to one core through a signalfd (Linux) or kqueue `EVFILT_SIGNAL` (darwin) and forwarded by relay; spawn with posix_spawn semantics because `fork` in a multi-threaded process is unsafe; `sendfile` integrated with anvil's output path for file responses. **Needs:** shapes for `io` on pipes; tasks for waiting on child processes. **Done when:** `os/signal`, `os/exec` and an anvil file response via `sendfile` pass tests on Linux and macOS, and a child process's output is read without blocking the core.
- [ ] TLS in the runtime's I/O path (non-blocking handshake, session resumption, kTLS)
  **Work:** integrate TLS into `wire` and anvil so handshakes and record processing are non-blocking, with session resumption and optional kernel TLS offload on Linux. **Why:** COVERAGE `crypto/tls` is missing and blocks HTTPS, WSS and TLS to databases (#124); the postgres client documents TLS as unsupported. **How:** the protocol work is in 12.3 and split in 14.4; here the runtime part: the handshake runs as a task step that parks on socket readiness, CPU-heavy handshake math may go to the offload pool (14.1), and kTLS hands the record layer to the kernel after the handshake. **Needs:** the crypto prerequisites in 14.3 (AES and carry-less multiply intrinsics, streaming hashes, asn1, x509). **Done when:** anvil serves HTTPS and the HTTP client fetches HTTPS URLs with handshakes that do not block other requests on the core (a handshake-storm test), and kTLS is used when available.
- [ ] Graceful reload and zero-downtime restart (socket handoff)
  **Work:** restart a server binary without dropping connections: the new process inherits listening sockets, the old one drains. **Why:** graceful shutdown already exists (PORTING.md section 4), but deploys still close listeners; zero-downtime restarts are expected of production servers. **How:** pass listener descriptors to the child via an environment convention or `SCM_RIGHTS` over a Unix socket, let the old process stop accepting and finish in-flight requests within a deadline; with `SO_REUSEPORT` on Linux the new process can also bind alongside. **Needs:** Unix sockets in `net`, process spawning. **Done when:** a CI test restarts a server under load and wrk reports zero socket errors.

### 4. Performance programme (continuous)

Performance is the end goal (docs/PERFORMANCE.md). Every claim in this section must be a number on named hardware with a method (14.5).

- [ ] A benchmark suite in the repo with Go, Rust and Odin baselines, run in CI on dedicated hardware, regressions block merges
  **Work:** one benchmark suite with baselines in Go, Rust and Odin, run on dedicated machines with results stored per commit. **Why:** today `bench/v2` has 13 CPU programs with Go twins and HTTP scripts run by hand (TOOLING.md section 7); the CI benchmark workflow is on demand and never a merge gate (docs/CI.md), so regressions are found late. **How:** at least 30 named programs (14.5), each with identical output across languages, run with repeats and a confidence interval on dedicated arm64 and amd64 machines; the 2 percent gate (12.5) applies only on that hardware. **Needs:** dedicated runners. **Done when:** every merge to main records results, a regression beyond the threshold fails the check, and a dashboard shows the history.
- [ ] The service benchmark of v0.4 measured on a quiet machine (wrk2: req/s and p99 against Go with chi), published
  **Work:** run `bench/v04` (GET /users/{id} through Redis over MySQL, Tin vs Go + chi, wrk2) on a quiet machine and publish the numbers in PERFORMANCE.md. **Why:** v0.4's acceptance criterion is that Tin wins on req/s and p99 including a slow/fast mix; the harness is built but unmeasured (issue #74). **How:** `bench/v04/run.py` with Redis and MySQL seeded by `seed.py`, on a machine with no other load, server and load generator on separate CPUs, several rounds. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** PERFORMANCE.md has the table (max req/s, req per CPU-second, p50/p99/p99.9 at fixed rates, RSS) and #74 is closed.
- [ ] Per-package micro benchmarks: strings, strconv, math, sort, maps, json, http parsing, hashing, compression
  **Work:** a benchmark per hot function in each named package, with a Go twin. **Why:** PERFORMANCE.md already found that gauge is 1.2 to 1.8x slower and generic sort 1.28x slower than Go; micro benchmarks localize regressions and target compiler work. **How:** `BenchmarkXxx` functions run by `tin test -bench` next to Go benchmarks over the same inputs, results compared with a `benchstat`-style tool (section 5). **Needs:** the benchstat-style comparison in `tin test`. **Done when:** each named package has benchmarks for its top functions and a report lists Tin/Go ratios per function.
- [ ] Performance budget documented per stdlib package (allocations per call, bytes copied)
  **Work:** state, per package, the allocations and copies each function may make, and test them. **Why:** "nothing hidden" (design_foundations principle 1) means costs must be visible; request pools make allocation cheap but memory lives until the request ends, so an unexpected allocation in a loop grows the pool. **How:** an allocation counter in the runtime readable from tests (`crucible` gains an `AllocsPerRun`-style helper), budgets written in each package doc, checked by tests. **Needs:** the runtime counter. **Done when:** every high-demand package documents its budget and a test fails when a function allocates more than stated.
- [ ] JSON: faster than the Go standard library and than `sonic`-class libraries on real-world payloads
  **Work:** make argo (encode and decode) beat Go's `encoding/json` and the fastest Go JSON libraries on a named set of real payloads. **Why:** argo's generated encoders are already 0.59x of Go's time on the bench/v2 encode benchmark; JSON dominates API servers' CPU. 14.4 asks for a baseline and margin first. **How:** pick payloads (Twitter, CITM, canada, GitHub events, typical API responses), measure decode as well as encode, add SIMD scanning (section 2) and the derivation rewrite without losing speed. **Needs:** SIMD kernels, derivation. **Done when:** on the named payloads Tin's encode and decode are faster than Go's standard library by a stated margin and at least equal to the fastest Go library, on both CPUs.
- [ ] HTTP server: beat Go's net/http and fasthttp on throughput and tail latency, with TLS
  **Work:** keep anvil ahead of net/http and fasthttp on req/s and p99, and extend the comparison to TLS. **Why:** anvil leads on one core (316k vs 231k vs 138k req/s on macOS, PERFORMANCE.md section 1) but the 4-core plaintext numbers are close to fasthttp, and no TLS numbers exist. **How:** the existing `bench/http` scripts plus TLS once 12.3's TLS work lands; profile with the built-in profiler. **Needs:** TLS. **Done when:** published results show anvil ahead on req/s and p99 at 1, 2 and 4 cores, plaintext and TLS, on Linux arm64 and amd64.
- [ ] Database clients: fewer allocations than pgx and go-sql-driver at equal features
