  **Work:** measure and minimize allocations per query in the mysql and postgres clients against pgx and go-sql-driver/mysql. **Why:** the clients are pooled per core and build rows in the task's pool (RUNTIME.md), which should already allocate less than Go's; the claim needs numbers. **How:** a benchmark of point queries, multi-row queries and inserts against a local server, counting allocations (pool bytes) and CPU per query on both sides. **Needs:** the runtime allocation counter. **Done when:** published numbers show fewer allocations and less CPU per query at equal features.
- [ ] Startup time and binary size budgets enforced in CI
  **Work:** ceilings for startup time and executable size, checked in CI. **Why:** hello world is 35 KB and the API server 91 KB on macOS against Go's 2.5 MB and 8.2 MB (PERFORMANCE.md section 4); these are selling points that silently erode without a gate. **How:** 14.5 names the programs (hello world, an HTTP echo server, the compiler) and asks for a ceiling each; measure size in CI and startup with repeated runs. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** CI fails when a ceiling is exceeded, and PERFORMANCE.md lists the ceilings.

### 5. Tooling (year 1 to 6)

The `tin` command is a shell script today (`./tin`, TOOLING.md section 2) with run, build, asm, test, suite, bootstrap and version.

- [ ] `tin` command: build, run, test, bench, fmt, vet, doc, get, mod, clean, install, version, env
  **Work:** one `tin` command covering the whole workflow, written in Tin. **Why:** the current script handles build, run, asm, test, suite, bootstrap and version; Go users expect fmt, vet, doc, module and env commands, and writing the driver in Tin follows the project's direction (Tin written in Tin, no new Python tools). **How:** a Tin program that calls the compiler as a library or subprocess, with subcommands added as their features land (fmt, vet, doc, packages from #146). **Needs:** the features behind each subcommand. **Done when:** the shell script is replaced by a Tin binary, every listed subcommand exists with `--help`, and the existing CI keeps working through it.
- [ ] `tin fmt`: one canonical format, stable, with a style check in CI
  **Work:** a formatter that prints any strict Tin file in one canonical layout. **Why:** one format ends style debates and diff noise; 14.3 moves it to year 1 because syntax is still moving and a formatter makes mechanical migrations possible. **How:** a printer over the parser's AST that keeps comments (the lexer must retain them), idempotent by test, with a `--check` mode used in CI on `lib/` and `tests/`. **Needs:** comment-preserving parsing. **Done when:** formatting every file in `lib/` twice gives the same result as once, the outputs compile to identical binaries, and CI rejects unformatted code.
- [ ] `tin vet`: the compiler's lints (unused, shadowing, suspicious formatting, misuse of `keep`)
  **Work:** a lint pass for likely bugs that are not errors: unused values and imports, shadowed variables, format strings whose verbs do not match argument types, unnecessary or missing `keep`. **Why:** the compiler already rejects ignored faults; lints catch the next class of mistakes without making them errors. **How:** passes over the checked tree, reusing the type and region information; each lint has a code and can be silenced per line. **Needs:** diagnostic codes. **Done when:** `tin vet` runs clean on `lib/` and each lint has positive and negative tests.
- [ ] `tin doc`: documentation from comments, searchable, with examples that run as tests
  **Work:** generate package documentation from comments, browse it from the command line and as HTML, and run `ExampleXxx` functions as tests with their expected output. **Why:** `tools/gendoc.py` writes docs/STDLIB.md from one-line comments today; moving it into Tin removes a Python tool and examples-as-tests keep docs true. **How:** reuse the parser to read declarations and comments; examples compare stdout with an `// Output:` comment as in Go. **Needs:** comment-preserving parsing (shared with fmt). **Done when:** STDLIB.md is produced by `tin doc`, `gendoc.py` is retired, and examples run in `tin test`.
- [ ] `tin test`: table tests, subtests, parallel tests, golden files, coverage, race-free by construction, fuzzing, benchmarks with `benchstat`-style comparison
  **Work:** complete the test runner and `crucible`: subtests with names and cleanup, parallel tests (as tasks), golden-file helpers, coverage reports, fuzz targets, and benchmark comparison between runs. **Why:** COVERAGE `testing` is partial (checks, Run, benchmarks; no t.Parallel, subtests with cleanup, TempDir, fuzzing, example tests); tests are the most imported thing in Go test files. "Race-free by construction" holds because parallel subtests are tasks on one core. **How:** subtests on `crucible.Run`, parallel tests as children of a scope, coverage by compiler-inserted counters, fuzzing with a mutation engine and corpus directory, `-count` and a statistical comparison of benchmark runs. **Needs:** closures and tasks for parallel subtests. **Done when:** each feature has a self-test, `testing`'s common API has a `crucible` equivalent, and coverage output is readable by a standard viewer.
- [ ] Language server (LSP): diagnostics, completion, go-to-definition, rename, hover, code actions, inlay hints
  **Work:** a language server for editors, written in Tin over the compiler's front end. **Why:** editor support decides adoption; diagnostics with spans and fix-its (section 2) become code actions. **How:** run lex/parse/check incrementally per file, keep symbol tables for definitions and references, speak JSON-RPC over stdio. **Needs:** diagnostic codes and spans; a front end that can check without generating code; the build cache for speed. **Done when:** VS Code and Neovim show live errors, completion, definitions, rename and hover on the standard library with sub-100 ms responses on a large file.
- [ ] Debugger support: DWARF, `lldb` and `gdb` pretty-printers, a Tin-aware debugger adapter (DAP)
  **Work:** make native debuggers useful: DWARF types and locations, pretty-printers for str, slices, maps, optionals, enums and faults, and a DAP adapter for editors. **Why:** today `lldb` has function names only and `tools/tinbt.py` walks frame pointers by hand (TOOLING.md section 8). **How:** DWARF from section 2, Python pretty-printers that decode the layouts of RUNTIME.md section 1 (the str header, the 32-byte slice header, the 80-byte map header), a DAP adapter driving lldb. **Needs:** DWARF variables. **Done when:** stepping through a Tin program in VS Code shows locals with readable values on macOS and Linux.
- [ ] Profilers: CPU, heap (pool usage), task and latency traces; flame graphs; `tin pprof`
  **Work:** command-line access to the runtime's profiles: CPU sampling, pool and ingot usage by site, task scheduling traces and request latency breakdowns, rendered as flame graphs. **Why:** COVERAGE lists `runtime/pprof`, `net/http/pprof` and `runtime/trace` as missing and calls them part of the performance goal. **How:** the runtime emits pprof-format profiles (section 3); `tin pprof` reads them or delegates to the standard pprof viewer; traces record task park/wake events per core. **Needs:** observability in the runtime; line tables. **Done when:** a profile of the HTTP benchmark shows the expected hot functions with lines, and a task trace shows each request's park/wake timeline.
- [ ] Package manager: resolution, lock file, checksums, vendoring, private registries, offline mode, mirror (#146)
  **Work:** the command-line side of packages: `tin get`, `tin vendor`, lock file updates, checksum verification, private sources, offline builds and mirrors. **Why:** design_foundations section 8 decides the model (exact content-addressed pins, vendored source, capabilities); the tool must make it convenient. "Resolution" here means fetching exactly what `tin.lock` pins, not semantic version solving. **How:** fetch by URL or mirror, verify hashes against the lock file, copy into `vendor/`, show capability changes on upgrade; a registry is an optional index on top (not a prerequisite). **Needs:** #146 in the compiler. **Done when:** a project with dependencies from two sources and a mirror builds offline from `vendor/`, and an upgrade that adds a capability is shown before it is accepted.
- [ ] Package registry and documentation site
  **Work:** a public index of packages with their documentation, hashes and capabilities. **Why:** discovery and documentation help an ecosystem grow; design_foundations section 8 deliberately makes the registry a later policy layer, not the source of truth (the lock file is). **How:** an index of URLs and content hashes, docs rendered by `tin doc`, capability lists shown per version; written in Tin and served by anvil. **Needs:** the package manager; `tin doc`; editions (14.2 says before the registry). **Done when:** packages can be published and found, and every listed version's hash matches its source.
- [ ] Editor support: VS Code, JetBrains, Neovim, Helix, Zed; tree-sitter grammar; syntax highlighting everywhere GitHub renders
  **Work:** a tree-sitter grammar, a TextMate grammar, and editor plugins wired to the LSP. **Why:** highlighting on GitHub (through linguist) and in editors is the first thing a new user sees. **How:** derive the tree-sitter grammar from LANGUAGE.md section 19, test it against every file in `tests/v2` and `lib/`, submit to linguist once usage qualifies. **Needs:** the LSP for plugin features. **Done when:** the grammar parses every strict file without errors and plugins exist for the listed editors.
- [ ] Playground in the browser (wasm)
  **Work:** a web page that compiles and runs Tin programs in the browser. **Why:** a playground lowers the cost of trying the language and is where docs examples run. **How:** compile the compiler itself to wasm and run outputs as wasm (needs the wasm target), or run a sandboxed server-side compile at first. **Needs:** the WebAssembly target (section 2). **Done when:** the tour's examples run in the browser with their expected output.
- [ ] Code generation tools in Tin (stringer-like, mocks via shapes, protobuf, OpenAPI, SQL)
  **Work:** generators for enum string methods, test doubles for shapes, protobuf and OpenAPI bindings, and typed SQL access. **Why:** much Go tooling is code generation; in Tin some of it is replaced by derivation at compile time (#145), and the rest should be Tin programs, not Python. **How:** prefer derivers (compile-time) where the input is a Tin type; use generators only for external schemas (`.proto`, OpenAPI, SQL), run through `tin generate`. **Needs:** derivation; shapes for mocks. **Done when:** each generator has a test that generates, compiles and runs code against a sample schema.
- [ ] Migration tooling: a Go-to-Tin translator for the common subset, and a report of what does not map
  **Work:** a tool that translates Go source to Tin where the mapping is mechanical and reports the rest (goroutines, interfaces with type switches, reflection, mutexes). **Why:** most target users have Go code; COVERAGE already maps each Go feature to its Tin form, which is the translation table. **How:** parse Go (with Go's own parser, run as a separate tool outside the build, since Go stays only as a comparison baseline) and emit Tin, mapping `int` to `i64`, `error` results to `!T`, `context` parameters to ambient context, `interface` to shapes. **Needs:** the foundations, so most constructs have a target. **Done when:** a sample of real Go packages translates with a report, and translated stdlib-only programs compile and match Go's output.
- [ ] Continuous integration templates and a hosted build cache
  **Work:** ready-made CI configurations for Tin projects and a shared content-addressed build cache. **Why:** users should get bootstrap-free, cached builds in CI without writing scripts; the repo's own CI (docs/CI.md) is the model. **How:** GitHub Actions and GitLab templates that install a pinned toolchain via the installer, run `tin test`, `tin vet` and `tin fmt --check`; the cache keyed by the compiler's content hash. **Needs:** the build cache; `tinup`. **Done when:** a template project goes green on a fresh repository and a second run uses the cache.
- [ ] Installers: Homebrew, apt and rpm repositories, container images, `tinup` for toolchain versions
  **Work:** package the toolchain for the usual channels and a version manager. **Why:** today there is a checksum-verifying `install.sh`, release archives and a multi-arch builder image (DISTRIBUTION.md); package managers and a version manager are expected. **How:** a Homebrew formula, signed apt and rpm repositories, slim runtime images, and `tinup` (the installer's version handling, `~/.tin/versions/`, turned into a command). **Needs:** signed releases (section 6). **Done when:** `brew install tin`, `apt install tin` and `tinup install 0.x` work and are tested in CI.

### 6. Safety and security (continuous)

- [ ] A memory-safety statement and proof sketch for the region checker; external review
  **Work:** a public statement of what Tin guarantees (no use after reset, no out-of-bounds, no data race, no uninitialized reads; LANGUAGE.md section 17) and what it does not (standard-library raw operations, integer overflow, stack overflow), with a proof sketch, reviewed by an outside expert. **Why:** Tin replaces a garbage collector with a compile-time checker; users and security reviewers need to know the guarantee's boundaries. **How:** build on the checker proof work of section 2 and the mechanized core calculus of 14.4; commission a review. **Needs:** the region proofs; closures and tasks finished (they change the rules). **Done when:** the statement is published in docs and the review's findings are fixed or documented.
- [ ] Sanitizer-grade debug mode (poisoned pools, canaries, use-after-reset detection at run time)
  **Work:** a debug build in which reset pools are poisoned and unmapped or protected, allocations carry canaries, and access to reset memory traps. **Why:** standard-library code uses raw operations the checker cannot see (LANGUAGE.md section 18), and checker bugs would show as use-after-reset; a runtime check catches both. **How:** in debug mode, never reuse pool chunks (map fresh ones and `mprotect` old ones), fill freed ingot blocks with a pattern and check it on reuse, add guard words after allocations. **Needs:** the mmap-based allocator. **Done when:** a test that deliberately keeps a reference past reset (through a raw operation) traps in debug mode with a report, and the whole suite passes in debug mode.
- [ ] Fuzz every parser in the library (JSON, HTTP, URL, TLS records, database wire protocols, archive formats)
  **Work:** fuzz targets for every parser that reads untrusted input. **Why:** these are the attack surface of a server; anvil's HTTP parser, argo, link, the redis/mysql/postgres decoders and future TLS and archive readers must never crash, hang or misparse. **How:** fuzz targets in `tin test` (section 5) with corpora seeded from existing tests and conformance suites; differential fuzzing against Go where a Go twin exists (link against net/url, argo against encoding/json). **Needs:** fuzzing in `tin test`. **Done when:** each listed parser has a fuzz target running nightly with no open crashes.
- [ ] Constant-time guarantees for the crypto package, tested with timing harnesses
  **Work:** guarantee that secret-dependent crypto code has no secret-dependent branches or memory accesses, and test it. **Why:** `seal.ConstantTimeEq` exists, and HMAC, PBKDF2 and future AES/ECC must not leak timing; an optimizing compiler can reintroduce branches (14.2 asks for codegen rules before SSA). **How:** a compiler-respected marker for constant-time functions (no branch-introducing optimizations, `csel` preserved), dudect-style statistical timing tests, and binary inspection of the hot functions. **Needs:** the constant-time codegen rules of 14.2. **Done when:** timing harnesses pass for every secret-handling function on both CPUs and are re-run after every optimizer change.
- [ ] Supply chain: signed releases, reproducible builds, SBOM, lock-file verification, capability prompts for dependencies
  **Work:** sign release artifacts, make them reproducible, publish a software bill of materials, verify lock files, and show capability changes when dependencies change. **Why:** releases are checksum-verified today (DISTRIBUTION.md) but not signed; packages with capabilities (design_foundations section 8) make dependency review concrete. **How:** sigstore or minisign signatures in the release workflow, reproducibility from section 2, an SBOM generated from `tin.lock`, and `tin get` printing capability diffs. **Needs:** reproducible builds; packages. **Done when:** a release can be verified by signature and rebuilt bit-identically, and `tin get` shows capability changes.
- [ ] Vulnerability policy, advisory database and `tin audit`
  **Work:** a security policy (how to report, response times), a database of advisories for Tin and its packages, and a command that checks a lock file against it. **Why:** production users need to know when a dependency or the standard library has a known issue. **How:** advisories keyed by package path and content hash ranges, `tin audit` matching `tin.lock`. **Needs:** packages. **Done when:** a SECURITY policy is published and `tin audit` flags a test advisory.
- [ ] FIPS-style validated crypto build, if customers need it
  **Work:** a build mode using a validated crypto module, only if a customer requires it. **Why:** regulated deployments require FIPS 140 validated crypto; COVERAGE marks Go's `crypto/fips140` switch as n/a because there is no module yet. **How:** isolate the crypto implementations into a module boundary that could be submitted for validation; decide when a customer asks. **Needs:** the crypto package complete and constant-time tested. **Done when:** either the decision "not needed" is recorded, or a validated module build exists.

### 7. Ecosystem and community (year 2 to 10)

- [ ] Language specification, tour, book, cookbook, migration guide from Go
  **Work:** the learning material: a versioned spec (section 1), an interactive tour, a book, task recipes, and a guide for Go programmers. **Why:** docs/LANGUAGE.md and the AGENT_PRIMER are references; newcomers need guided material, and the Go migration guide (built from COVERAGE's mapping) is the main on-ramp. **How:** examples are tested by the suite (14.6); the tour runs in the playground. **Needs:** the foundations settled; the playground for the tour. **Done when:** each document exists, is versioned with the language and its examples run in CI.
- [ ] Style guide and project layout guide
  **Work:** conventions for naming (Tin's short-word package names), errors, faults and sentinels, package layout, tests and comments. **Why:** "one way to do it" (design_foundations principle 5) extends to style; the formatter fixes layout but not naming or structure. **How:** written from the standard library's practice; lints in `tin vet` where a rule is checkable. **Needs:** `tin fmt` and `tin vet`. **Done when:** the guide is published and the standard library follows it.
- [ ] Governance: RFC process, editions, release cadence, long-term support releases
  **Work:** how language changes are proposed and decided, how often releases ship, and which ones get long-term support. **Why:** contributors need a process, and users need predictability; editions (14.2) are the mechanism for breaking changes. **How:** an RFC repository with templates mirroring the design_foundations format (need, decision, replaces, rejected, unlocks); a fixed release cadence; LTS releases with backports (14.6 release engineering). **Needs:** editions. **Done when:** the process is documented and at least one change has gone through it.
- [ ] A foundation or an equivalent home for the project; trademark and license policy
  **Work:** a legal home for the project, trademark rules for the name, and a clear license policy for contributions. **Why:** companies adopt languages whose future does not depend on one person or employer. **How:** choose an existing foundation or form one; contributor license or DCO policy. **Needs:** production users and contributors. **Done when:** the project's home, trademark policy and contribution terms are published.
- [ ] Third-party libraries to encourage: web frameworks, ORMs, queue clients (Kafka, NATS, SQS, RabbitMQ), cloud SDKs, observability agents, gRPC, GraphQL
  **Work:** seed and support the libraries real services need, outside the standard library. **Why:** a language is adopted when its usual stack exists; section 10 lists what the project itself should provide. **How:** publish design guidance (use shapes, derivation, ambient context, per-core pools), offer review and promotion, maintain a list. **Needs:** packages and the registry; the foundations. **Done when:** each named category has at least one maintained library that passes its own tests against real services.
- [ ] Production references: Large production services running in Tin, with published numbers
  **Work:** get services into production and publish their numbers (throughput, latency, memory, cost). **Why:** real deployments prove the claims and find the gaps benchmarks miss; 14.3 makes two external production services a prerequisite for spec 1.0. **How:** work with early adopters, starting with a service of the yardstick kind; collect before/after metrics. **Needs:** the year-2 exit criteria (context, TLS, database shape, HTTP complete, LSP, formatter). **Done when:** at least two external services run in production with published numbers.
- [ ] Conferences, training material and certification
  **Work:** talks, workshops, course material and possibly a certification. **Why:** community growth and hiring depend on people being able to learn and prove skills. **How:** start with talks on the design (regions, share-nothing, shapes), then workshops built from the tour. **Needs:** stable language and docs. **Done when:** a training course exists and has been delivered.
- [ ] Compatibility with Go tooling where useful (`go list`-like metadata, SARIF reports)
  **Work:** emit project metadata in a `go list`-like JSON form and diagnostics as SARIF. **Why:** CI systems and code scanning tools already consume these formats, so Tin projects plug in without new integrations. **How:** `tin list -json` describing packages, files and dependencies; `tin vet -sarif`. **Needs:** packages; diagnostic codes. **Done when:** GitHub code scanning shows Tin diagnostics from a SARIF upload.

### 8. Years, in short

| Year | Theme | Exit criteria |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (2026 to 2027) | Foundations and breadth | Sections 1 foundations done; stdlib "high demand" packages done and verified; libc gone on Linux; the service benchmark published |
| 2 | Production readiness | `context`, TLS, database/sql shape, HTTP client and server complete; LSP and formatter; first external service in production |
| 3 | Performance leadership | SSA middle end, inliner, intrinsics, SIMD kernels; Tin ahead of Go on the benchmark suite; package manager and registry live |
| 4 | Platforms | Windows, darwin-amd64, wasm; debugger and profiler complete |
| 5 | Ecosystem | Third-party libraries for the usual stacks; spec 1.0 and the compatibility promise |
| 6 to 8 | Depth | Second backend, PGO and LTO by default, formal checker proofs, FIPS build, embedded targets |
| 9 to 10 | Maturity | Long-term support, foundation governance, the standard library at parity with Go's and ahead where Tin's design allows |

### 9. Standard library, A to Z

One box per Go standard-library package (the 176 that `go list std` reports for Go 1.26, as in docs/COVERAGE.md), ordered by import path. `[x]` means done; the note says what Tin package carries it and what is still missing. The indented sentence under each box says what Go's package does, what Tin has now (from the COVERAGE row) and the next concrete step; a box is checked only when the package is verified against Go (notes/stdlib_verified.md) or the gap is a documented, tested difference.

- [ ] `archive/tar`: missing; tar archives; needs the io shape first
  Go's `archive/tar` reads and writes tar archives as a stream of headers and file bodies; Tin has nothing, and the next step, once the `io` shapes land, is a `tar` package with a Reader and Writer over any `Reader`/`Writer` (USTAR, PAX and GNU headers), verified by round trips and by reading archives Go wrote.
- [ ] `archive/zip`: missing; zip archives; needs compress/flate
  Go's `archive/zip` reads and writes zip files with a central directory and random access through `ReaderAt`; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a zip package on the `io` shapes (`ReaderAt`, `Writer`) once `compress/flate` exists, verified by cross-reading archives with Go.
- [ ] `bufio` (flume): partial; buffered Reader (Line, Byte, ReadAll) and Writer (Str, Int, Flush); no Scanner with split functions, no ReadWriter
  Go's `bufio` wraps any reader or writer with a buffer and adds `Scanner` with split functions (lines, words, runes); Tin's `flume` has a concrete buffered Reader (Line, Byte, ReadAll) and Writer (Str, Int, Flush) on files, and the next step is to make flume generic over the `Reader`/`Writer` shapes and add `Scanner` with split functions (closures) and `ReadWriter`, with a Go twin.
- [ ] `bytes` (ore, twine.Builder): partial; about 20 functions on []u8; no Buffer or Reader type, no Map, Title, FieldsFunc or TrimFunc
  Go's `bytes` mirrors `strings` for `[]byte` and adds `Buffer` and `Reader`; Tin's `ore` has about 20 functions on `[]u8` and `twine.Builder` covers building, and the next step is to port twine's verified Unicode functions (Map, Title, FieldsFunc, TrimFunc and the rest) to `[]u8` and add `Buffer` and `Reader` satisfying the io shapes, verified with a twin like twine's 3,544-line one.
- [ ] `cmp` (sift (Less, Cmp), builtin min/max): partial; Less and Cmp (NaN first, as Go); no cmp.Or and no named Ordered constraint (a union such as `i64 | f64 | str` does the constraining)
  Go's `cmp` provides `Ordered`, `Compare`, `Less` and `Or`; Tin has `sift.Less` and `sift.Cmp` (NaN first, as Go) and two-argument `min`/`max`, and the next step is a named `Ordered` shape once named constraints exist (section 1) plus `cmp.Or`, verified against Go.
- [ ] `compress/bzip2`: missing
  Go's `compress/bzip2` is a bzip2 decompressor (no compressor); Tin has nothing, and the next step, low priority, is a decompressing Reader on the io shapes verified against files produced by the bzip2 tool and decoded by Go.
- [ ] `compress/flate`: missing; needed by gzip, zlib and zip
  Go's `compress/flate` implements DEFLATE (RFC 1951) compression levels and decompression; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a streaming inflater first (needed to read gzip responses), then a compressor with Go's levels, verified by cross-decoding with Go and benchmarked against it.
- [ ] `compress/gzip`: missing
  Go's `compress/gzip` wraps DEFLATE with the gzip header and CRC-32; Tin has nothing (CRC-32 exists in `stamp`), and the next step after flate is a gzip Reader and Writer, then transparent gzip in the HTTP client and an anvil compression middleware, verified against Go.
- [ ] `compress/lzw`: missing
  Go's `compress/lzw` implements the LZW variant used by GIF and TIFF; Tin has nothing, and the next step, needed only for `image/gif`, is a Reader and Writer verified against Go's output.
- [ ] `compress/zlib`: missing
  Go's `compress/zlib` wraps DEFLATE with the zlib header and Adler-32; Tin has nothing (Adler-32 exists in `stamp`), and the next step after flate is a zlib Reader and Writer (needed by `image/png`), verified against Go.
- [ ] `container/heap` (cairn): partial; IntHeap and IntMaxHeap; no heap over any element type (generics now allow one)
  Go's `container/heap` turns any `heap.Interface` into a priority queue; Tin's `cairn` has `IntHeap` and `IntMaxHeap` only, and the next step is a generic `Heap[T]` with a `less` function (a closure, or an `Ordered` constraint) offering Push, Pop, Fix and Remove, verified against Go's operation order.
- [ ] `container/list` (cairn (deque, queue)): missing; no doubly linked list with stable element handles
  Go's `container/list` is a doubly linked list with stable element handles; Tin's `cairn` has a deque and a queue but no list with handles, and the next step is a generic `List[T]` whose elements live in the owning region (handles as indexes so `keep` can copy it), with a Go twin.
- [ ] `container/ring`: missing
  Go's `container/ring` is a circular list; Tin has nothing, and the next step, low priority, is a small generic ring in `cairn` with a Go twin.
- [ ] `context` (design: ambient task deadline and cancellation): missing; every request task already has a deadline; the cancel signal, values and the scoped form are unbuilt
  Go's `context` carries deadlines, cancellation and request values through call chains; Tin's request tasks already have a deadline (`anvil.Deadline`), and the next step is the ambient design of #144 (`within`, typed `slot`/`with`, cancellation through `rt_task_wait`), plus a small interop shim with `Done()`/`Err()` for ported code.
- [-] `crypto`: n/a; the Hash registry and interfaces; there are no interfaces
  Go's `crypto` is the registry of hash algorithms and the `Signer`/`Decrypter` interfaces; Tin has no interfaces and no registry, so nothing is built: each hash is a concrete type satisfying the `hash` shape, and signing APIs are concrete per algorithm.
- [ ] `crypto/aes`: missing
  Go's `crypto/aes` is the AES block cipher with hardware acceleration; Tin has nothing, and the next step is AES using the AES instructions on arm64 and AES-NI on amd64 (intrinsics, 14.3) with a constant-time software fallback, verified against NIST and Wycheproof vectors.
- [ ] `crypto/cipher`: missing; GCM, CTR, CBC
  Go's `crypto/cipher` provides block modes and AEADs (GCM, CTR, CBC, OFB, CFB); Tin has nothing, and the next step after AES is GCM (with PMULL/PCLMUL carry-less multiply) and CTR for TLS, then CBC, verified against Wycheproof vectors.
- [ ] `crypto/des`: missing
  Go's `crypto/des` implements DES and triple DES for legacy systems; Tin has nothing, and the next step, low priority, is triple DES only if a legacy protocol needs it.
- [ ] `crypto/dsa`: missing; deprecated in Go
  Go's `crypto/dsa` implements the deprecated DSA signature scheme; Tin has nothing and plans nothing unless a legacy SSH or X.509 need appears.
- [ ] `crypto/ecdh`: missing
  Go's `crypto/ecdh` does key exchange over X25519 and the NIST curves; Tin has nothing, and the next step is X25519 and P-256 ECDH for TLS 1.3 key shares, constant time, verified against RFC 7748 and Wycheproof vectors.
- [ ] `crypto/ecdsa`: missing
  Go's `crypto/ecdsa` signs and verifies with ECDSA on the NIST curves; Tin has nothing, and the next step is P-256 verification (for X.509 chains and TLS), then signing with deterministic nonces, verified against Wycheproof.
- [ ] `crypto/ed25519`: missing
  Go's `crypto/ed25519` signs and verifies Ed25519; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a constant-time Ed25519 sharing field arithmetic with X25519, verified against RFC 8032 vectors.
- [ ] `crypto/elliptic`: missing
  Go's `crypto/elliptic` exposes NIST curve arithmetic (mostly deprecated in favour of `ecdh`); Tin has nothing, and the next step is internal P-256/384/521 arithmetic used by ecdh and ecdsa, without a public low-level API.
- [-] `crypto/fips140`: n/a; Go's FIPS module switch
  Go's `crypto/fips140` reports and controls Go's FIPS 140-3 mode; Tin has no validated module, so there is nothing to build unless the FIPS build of section 6 is undertaken.
- [ ] `crypto/hkdf`: missing
  Go's `crypto/hkdf` implements HKDF (RFC 5869) extract and expand; Tin has nothing (HMAC-SHA256 exists in `seal`), and the next step is HKDF over the streaming hash shape, needed by TLS 1.3's key schedule, verified against RFC vectors.
- [ ] `crypto/hmac` (seal): partial; HmacSha256 only
  Go's `crypto/hmac` computes HMAC over any hash and compares MACs in constant time; Tin's `seal` has `HmacSha256` only, and the next step is HMAC generic over the `hash` shape (SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512) with `Equal`, verified against RFC 4231 vectors.
- [ ] `crypto/hpke`: missing
  Go's `crypto/hpke` implements Hybrid Public Key Encryption (RFC 9180); Tin has nothing, and the next step, later, is HPKE on top of X25519, HKDF and AES-GCM once those exist.
- [ ] `crypto/md5` ((postgres/md5, internal)): partial; exists only inside the PostgreSQL client; not public
  Go's `crypto/md5` computes MD5 (for checksums, not security); Tin has an MD5 inside the postgres client for legacy authentication, and the next step is to move it into a public package with a streaming hash satisfying the `hash` shape, verified against RFC 1321 vectors (already checked in CI for the internal copy).
- [ ] `crypto/mlkem`: missing
  Go's `crypto/mlkem` implements the post-quantum ML-KEM key encapsulation (FIPS 203); Tin has nothing, and the next step, after TLS 1.3 works, is ML-KEM-768 for hybrid key exchange, verified against the NIST vectors.
- [-] `crypto/mlkem/mlkemtest`: n/a
  Go's `crypto/mlkem/mlkemtest` exposes deterministic ML-KEM functions for testing Go's own implementation; Tin needs no counterpart, since its tests will use the published vectors directly.
- [ ] `crypto/pbkdf2` (seal): partial; Pbkdf2Sha256 and a timeout form; no other hashes
  Go's `crypto/pbkdf2` derives keys with PBKDF2 over any hash; Tin's `seal` has `Pbkdf2Sha256` and a timeout form that yields between batches, and the next step is PBKDF2 generic over the `hash` shape (SHA-1, SHA-512), verified against RFC 6070-style vectors.
- [ ] `crypto/rand` (seal): partial; RandomBytes; no Reader, Int or Prime
  Go's `crypto/rand` provides a cryptographically secure `Reader`, `Int`, `Prime` and `Text`; Tin's `seal.RandomBytes` uses `arc4random_buf` on macOS and `getrandom` on Linux, and the next step is a `Reader` satisfying the io shape plus `Int` and `Prime` (needs `math/big`), verified by statistical checks.
- [ ] `crypto/rc4`: missing; deprecated in Go
  Go's `crypto/rc4` implements the broken RC4 stream cipher; Tin has nothing and plans nothing.
- [ ] `crypto/rsa` (seal): partial; ParseRSAPublicKeyPEM and EncryptOAEPSha1 (the MySQL login); no key generation, signing or verification
  Go's `crypto/rsa` generates keys and does PKCS #1 v1.5 and PSS signatures and OAEP encryption; Tin's `seal` has `ParseRSAPublicKeyPEM` and `EncryptOAEPSha1` for the MySQL login, and the next step is PSS and PKCS #1 v1.5 verification for X.509 and TLS (needs `math/big` or a fixed-width bignum), then signing and key generation, verified against Wycheproof.
- [ ] `crypto/sha1` (seal): partial; Sha1 one shot; no streaming hash
  Go's `crypto/sha1` computes SHA-1 one shot or streaming; Tin's `seal` has a one-shot `Sha1`, and the next step is a streaming `Sha1` type satisfying the `hash` shape (with the SHA-1 instructions on arm64), verified against FIPS vectors.
- [ ] `crypto/sha256` (seal): partial; Sha256, Sha256Hex (hardware instructions where present); no streaming hash, no SHA-224
  Go's `crypto/sha256` computes SHA-224 and SHA-256 one shot or streaming; Tin's `seal` has `Sha256` and `Sha256Hex` using the SHA-256 instructions where present (1.05x Go on 100 MB), and the next step is a streaming type on the `hash` shape plus SHA-224, with SHA-NI on amd64, verified against FIPS vectors.
- [ ] `crypto/sha3`: missing
  Go's `crypto/sha3` implements SHA-3 and the SHAKE extendable-output functions; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a Keccak-based package on the `hash` shape (needed by ML-KEM), verified against NIST vectors.
- [ ] `crypto/sha512`: missing
  Go's `crypto/sha512` computes SHA-384 and SHA-512 and their truncations; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a streaming SHA-512/384 on the `hash` shape (needed by TLS cipher suites and Ed25519), with SHA-512 instructions on arm64 where present, verified against FIPS vectors.
- [ ] `crypto/subtle` (seal): partial; ConstantTimeEq only
  Go's `crypto/subtle` provides constant-time comparisons, selection and XOR; Tin's `seal` has `ConstantTimeEq`, and the next step is `ConstantTimeCompare`, `ConstantTimeSelect`, `ConstantTimeByteEq` and `XORBytes`, protected by the constant-time codegen rules of 14.2 and timing tests.
- [ ] `crypto/tls`: missing; issue #124: client first, then server; blocks https, wss and TLS to databases
  Go's `crypto/tls` implements TLS 1.2 and 1.3 clients and servers; Tin has nothing (#124), and the next step is the split in 14.4: record layer, then a TLS 1.3 client with X.509 verification against system roots, integrated non-blocking into `wire` (section 3), after the prerequisites in 14.3.
- [ ] `crypto/x509`: missing
  Go's `crypto/x509` parses certificates, keys and CSRs and verifies chains against roots; Tin has nothing, and the next step is DER certificate parsing (needs `encoding/asn1`), chain building and verification with name constraints, and loading system roots per OS, verified against Go on a corpus of real chains.
- [ ] `crypto/x509/pkix`: missing
  Go's `crypto/x509/pkix` holds the ASN.1 structures for names and extensions used by x509; Tin has nothing, and the next step is to define these structures inside the x509 work (derived ASN.1 decoders once derivation exists).
- [ ] `database/sql` (mysql, postgres (and the `query` type)): partial; each client has Open, Query, Exec, Begin, Commit, Rollback and typed values, pooled per core; no shared driver abstraction, no Scan into structs, no prepared-statement handle API
  Go's `database/sql` is a generic SQL API over drivers with connection pooling, `Scan`, transactions and prepared statements; Tin's `mysql` and `postgres` clients each have Open, Query, Exec, Begin, Commit, Rollback and typed values, pooled per core, with `query` literals that keep values apart from SQL text, and the next step is the shared shape of 12.3 (`Conn`, `Rows`, `Tx`, `Stmt`) with `Scan` into structs by derivation.
- [ ] `database/sql/driver`: design; no interfaces: a driver would be a package with a fixed shape or a table of functions
  Go's `database/sql/driver` is the set of interfaces a driver implements; Tin has no interfaces, and the next step is to express the driver contract as shapes (design_foundations section 2) that mysql and postgres satisfy structurally, used statically by default.
- [ ] `debug/buildinfo`: missing; low priority
  Go's `debug/buildinfo` reads the module and build settings embedded in a Go binary; Tin embeds no such record yet, and the next step, low priority, is to embed version and lock-file hash in binaries (with packages) and a reader for it.
- [ ] `debug/dwarf`: missing; low priority
  Go's `debug/dwarf` reads DWARF debug information; Tin has nothing, and the next step, after the compiler writes DWARF (section 2), is a reader useful for the runtime's own symbolization and tools, low priority otherwise.
- [ ] `debug/elf`: missing; low priority (the compiler writes ELF but does not read it)
  Go's `debug/elf` reads ELF files; the Tin compiler writes ELF (`elf.tin`, `elf_x64.tin`) but nothing reads it, and the next step, low priority, is a reader package useful for tools and vDSO parsing in the libc-free runtime.
- [-] `debug/gosym`: n/a; Go symbol tables
  Go's `debug/gosym` reads Go's own pclntab symbol tables; Tin binaries do not have them, so there is nothing to build.
- [ ] `debug/macho`: missing; low priority
  Go's `debug/macho` reads Mach-O files; the compiler writes Mach-O (`macho.tin`) but nothing reads it, and the next step, low priority, is a reader for tools.
- [ ] `debug/pe`: missing; low priority
  Go's `debug/pe` reads PE files; Tin has nothing, and the next step, after the Windows target's PE writer, is a reader for tools, low priority.
- [-] `debug/plan9obj`: n/a
  Go's `debug/plan9obj` reads Plan 9 object files; Tin does not target Plan 9, so there is nothing to build.
- [ ] `embed`: missing; compile-time file embedding
  Go's `embed` exposes files embedded at compile time as a string, bytes or an `embed.FS`; Tin has nothing, and the next step is the `//embed` work of section 1 (an attribute on a global resolved by the compiler, an `embed.FS` satisfying the `io/fs` shapes).
- [ ] `encoding` (compile-time derivation): design; Marshaler interfaces become derived code, as argo already does for JSON
  Go's `encoding` defines the `TextMarshaler` and `BinaryMarshaler` interfaces; Tin has no interfaces and argo already generates JSON code per type, and the next step is to express custom encodings as methods found through shapes and derivers (#145), so a type's own `MarshalText` is honoured by every encoder.
- [ ] `encoding/ascii85`: missing
  Go's `encoding/ascii85` implements the btoa/Adobe ASCII85 encoding; Tin has nothing, and the next step, low priority, is an encoder and decoder verified by round trips against Go.
- [ ] `encoding/asn1`: missing; needed by x509
  Go's `encoding/asn1` parses and writes DER using reflection; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a DER reader and writer with explicit parsing functions first (for x509 and TLS), then derived decoders through attributes, verified against Go on certificate corpora.
- [ ] `encoding/base32`: missing
  Go's `encoding/base32` implements RFC 4648 base32 (standard and hex alphabets, padding options); Tin has nothing, and the next step is a small package with both alphabets and padding control, verified against Go.
- [ ] `encoding/base64` (seal): partial; standard (padded) and URL-safe (unpadded) with decoders; no padded URL-safe form, no unpadded standard form, no streaming encoder
  Go's `encoding/base64` offers four encodings (standard and URL, padded and raw) plus streaming encoders; Tin's `seal` has standard padded and URL-safe unpadded with decoders, and the next step is all four variants, strict decoding options and a streaming encoder on the Writer shape, with SIMD kernels later, verified against Go.
- [ ] `encoding/binary`: missing; byte orders, varints, Read and Write of fixed-size values
  Go's `encoding/binary` reads and writes integers in little/big endian, varints and fixed-size structs; Tin has byte-order helpers only inside packages, and the next step is `LittleEndian`/`BigEndian` get/put/append functions and varints (single loads with `rev` intrinsics), then struct encoding by derivation, verified against Go.
- [ ] `encoding/csv`: missing
  Go's `encoding/csv` reads and writes RFC 4180 CSV; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a Reader and Writer on the io shapes with Go's quoting and `LazyQuotes` rules, verified against Go on edge cases, then row decoding by derivation.
- [ ] `encoding/gob`: missing; low priority: Go's own format
  Go's `encoding/gob` is Go's self-describing binary format built on reflection; Tin has nothing, and the next step is only a decision (14.7 marks it replaced by design), since cross-language services rarely need gob.
- [ ] `encoding/hex` (seal): partial; Hex and HexDecode; no Dump, no streaming
  Go's `encoding/hex` encodes and decodes hexadecimal and produces `hexdump`-style dumps; Tin's `seal` has `Hex` and `HexDecode`, and the next step is `Dump`, `Dumper`, streaming encoder and decoder on the io shapes and `AppendEncode`, verified against Go.
- [ ] `encoding/json` (argo): partial; Put and Get are generated per type, fast; no decoding into a dynamic value, no field tags, no Indent, no streaming Encoder or Decoder, no RawMessage beyond Raw
  Go's `encoding/json` marshals and unmarshals Go values with tags, streaming, indentation and dynamic values; Tin's `argo` generates fast encoders and decoders per type (0.59x Go's time on encode), and the next step is the 12.3 list: field attributes through derivation, a `json.Value` enum for dynamic data, `Indent`/`Compact`/`Valid`, and a streaming Decoder, verified on JSONTestSuite.
- [ ] `encoding/pem`: missing

  Go's `sort` sorts slices and anything implementing `sort.Interface`; Tin's `sift` has Ints, Strs, SortBy, the Search family and the generic Sort and SortFunc, and the next step is to close the remaining gaps (Float64s, `Stable`, `Find`) and document that `sort.Interface` and `sort.Slice` are replaced by generics and closures.
- [ ] `strconv` (mint): partial; Itoa, Atoi, ParseInt, ParseUint, ParseBool, ParseFloat, FormatInt, FormatUint, FormatFloat, Quote, Unquote and friends; no AppendFloat, AppendBool, QuoteToASCII, IsPrint, ParseComplex
  Go's `strconv` converts between strings and numbers and quotes strings; Tin's `mint` has Itoa, Atoi, the Parse and Format families, Quote and Unquote (identical to Go apart from returning zero values with range faults), and the next step is the Append forms, QuoteToASCII, QuoteToGraphic, IsPrint, IsGraphic and CanBackquote (12.3), with ParseComplex after the complex decision.
- [ ] `strings` (twine): partial; every function except the iterator forms and Reader: Index family, Split family with SplitAfter, Fields and FieldsFunc, Map, Title, Unicode ToUpper, ToLower, ToTitle, EqualFold by SimpleFold, Trim ...
  Go's `strings` manipulates UTF-8 strings and provides Builder, Reader and Replacer; Tin's `twine` has every function except the iterator forms, Reader and ToUpperSpecial (identical to Go on 3,544 lines), and the next step is `NewReader` on the io shapes and the `*Seq` iterator forms (Lines as an iterator).
- [-] `structs`: n/a
  Go's `structs` holds marker types such as `HostLayout` for struct layout control; Tin's struct layout is defined by its own rules (widest first), so there is nothing to build.
- [ ] `sync` (share-nothing cores, relay): design; no Mutex or RWMutex by design; WaitGroup, Once, Pool and Map need routine-level equivalents
  Go's `sync` provides mutexes, wait groups, once, pools and concurrent maps; Tin has share-nothing cores and `relay` and no mutexes by design, and the next step is the replacements of design_foundations section 6: scopes for WaitGroup, package initializers or per-core `once` for Once, the request pool for Pool, and per-core `atlas` plus relay for Map, documented with examples.
- [ ] `sync/atomic`: missing; the runtime has atomic operations as compiler intrinsics; there is no public package
  Go's `sync/atomic` provides atomic loads, stores, adds and compare-and-swap; Tin's runtime uses `__atomic_*` intrinsics privately, and the next step is the public `atomic` package with `I64`, `U64` and `Bool` (section 1), the only types allowed as written `shared var`.
- [ ] `syscall`: missing; low priority
  Go's `syscall` exposes raw OS system calls and constants; Tin's runtime has its own OS layer, and the next step, after libc removal, is to decide whether a public raw-syscall package exists (behind the `unsafe` capability) or system access stays inside typed packages.
- [ ] `testing` (crucible, `tin test`): partial; checks, Run, benchmarks; no t.Parallel, subtests with cleanup, TempDir, fuzzing, example tests
  Go's `testing` provides tests, benchmarks, fuzzing, subtests and helpers; Tin's `crucible` and `tin test` have checks, Run and benchmarks, and the next step is the section 5 list: subtests with cleanup, parallel tests as tasks, TempDir, Setenv, fuzzing and example tests.
- [ ] `testing/cryptotest`: missing
  Go's `testing/cryptotest` provides helpers for testing crypto implementations; Tin has nothing, and the next step is Wycheproof and NIST vector runners in crucible for the crypto packages.
- [ ] `testing/fstest`: missing
  Go's `testing/fstest` provides an in-memory file system and a conformance tester for `fs.FS`; Tin has nothing, and the next step after `io/fs` is a `MapFS` and `TestFS` equivalent.
- [ ] `testing/iotest`: missing
  Go's `testing/iotest` provides readers and writers that misbehave (one byte at a time, errors, timeouts) to test io code; Tin has nothing, and the next step after the io shapes is the same helpers.
- [ ] `testing/quick`: missing
  Go's `testing/quick` does property-based testing with random values via reflection; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a property-testing helper whose value generators are derived (#145) instead of reflected.
- [ ] `testing/slogtest`: missing
  Go's `testing/slogtest` checks that a slog handler behaves correctly; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a conformance test for herald handlers once handlers are a shape.
- [ ] `testing/synctest`: missing
  Go's `testing/synctest` runs goroutines in a bubble with a fake clock; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a test mode where a core's timers use a virtual clock, so tests of deadlines and tickers run instantly and deterministically.
- [ ] `text/scanner`: missing
  Go's `text/scanner` tokenizes Go-like source text; Tin has nothing, and the next step, low priority, is a small configurable tokenizer for config and DSL parsing.
- [ ] `text/tabwriter`: missing
  Go's `text/tabwriter` aligns columns of text; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a Writer on the io shapes with Go's elastic tabstop rules, verified against Go (useful for CLI tools).
- [ ] `text/template`: missing
  Go's `text/template` executes data-driven templates through reflection; Tin has nothing, and the next step is the template engine of section 10, which compiles templates at build time through derivation (14.7 notes it needs derivation first).
- [ ] `text/template/parse`: missing
  Go's `text/template/parse` builds parse trees for templates; Tin has nothing, and the next step is the parser inside the template engine, not a separate public API at first.
- [ ] `time` (tide): partial; Now, Since, Sleep, Wait, durations with parse and format, RFC 3339 and HTTP date, calendar arithmetic; no time zones or Location, no layout-based Format and Parse, no Timer, Ticker or After, no Mon...
  Go's `time` provides instants, durations, time zones, layout-based formatting and timers; Tin's `tide` has Now, Since, Sleep, Wait, durations with parse and format, RFC 3339 and HTTP dates and calendar arithmetic (identical to Go), and the next step is the 12.3 plan: Month and Weekday, Location from the tz database, layout-based Format and Parse, and Timer, Ticker and After on the scheduler.
- [ ] `time/tzdata`: missing
  Go's `time/tzdata` embeds the time zone database into the binary; Tin has no zones yet, and the next step after `Location` is an optional embedded database (using `embed`) for systems without `/usr/share/zoneinfo`.
- [ ] `unicode` (glyph): partial; Unicode 15.0.0 as Go has it: Is over every category, script and property (the Table enum), IsOneOf, IsLetter, IsDigit, IsNumber, IsSpace, IsUpper, IsLower, IsTitle, IsMark, IsPunct, IsSymbol, IsCon...
  Go's `unicode` provides Unicode classification, case mapping and range tables; Tin's `glyph` has Unicode 15.0.0 as Go has it (Is over every table, the Is* functions, To, ToUpper, ToLower, ToTitle and SimpleFold, identical on 258 lines), and the next step is RangeTable values, SpecialCase (Turkish casing) and FoldCategory/FoldScript.
- [ ] `unicode/utf16`: missing
  Go's `unicode/utf16` encodes and decodes UTF-16 surrogate pairs; Tin has nothing, and the next step is Encode, Decode, AppendRune and the surrogate helpers (needed for JSON `\u` escapes and Windows), verified against Go.
- [x] `unicode/utf8` (glyph): done; every function
  Go's `unicode/utf8` encodes, decodes and validates UTF-8; Tin's `glyph` has every function, and the next step is only the SIMD validation kernel of section 2 for speed.
- [ ] `unique`: missing
  Go's `unique` interns comparable values into handles that compare by pointer; Tin has nothing, and the next step is a per-core interning table in the ingot heap (values must be `keep`able), since without a collector handles are never reclaimed unless the long-lived-heap policy of 14.1 provides a way.
- [ ] `unsafe`: design; raw operations exist only for the standard library, behind the region checker
  Go's `unsafe` allows pointer arithmetic and type punning; Tin allows raw operations only in `lib/` (LANGUAGE.md section 18), and the next step is the audited raw-memory package of section 1, importable outside `lib/` only with the `unsafe` capability.
- [-] `weak`: n/a; there is no garbage collector
  Go's `weak` provides weak pointers that the garbage collector clears; Tin has no collector, so there is nothing to build (caches use explicit eviction under the 14.1 policy instead).

`[-]` marks a package that is specific to Go's toolchain or runtime and has no counterpart to build.

### 10. Beyond Go's library (Tin-native)

These packages go past Go's standard library where Tin's design (per-core state, request pools, derivation, ambient context) gives a better form, or where services always need them.

- [ ] `link`, `atlas`, `bits`, `sift`, `glyph`: keep API parity with Go and add Tin-native forms (iterators, shapes, derivation)
  **Work:** keep these verified packages identical to Go as Go evolves, and add the forms the foundations enable: iterator variants (`atlas.All`, `sift.Values`), shape-based APIs (`sift.Ordered`), and derived encodings (`link.URL` to and from JSON). **Why:** each is verified against Go (notes/stdlib_verified.md), and parity is only worth something if it is maintained; Tin-native forms are where they can be better than Go. **How:** regenerate the twins when Go releases change behaviour, add new forms with their own twin cases. **Needs:** iterators, shapes, derivation. **Done when:** twins pass against the latest Go release and each package has its iterator or shape forms with tests.
- [ ] `herald`: structured logging on par with slog, with sampling and async sinks
  **Work:** make herald a complete structured logger: handlers, groups, JSON and text output, per-level sampling, and sinks that write without blocking the core. **Why:** COVERAGE marks `log/slog` partial (no Handler, Group or LogValuer); logging on the request path must not block, and a share-nothing design suggests per-core buffers flushed by a helper. **How:** per-core buffers, a flush through the helper threads or a dedicated core, request id and trace id read from context slots, sampling by key; handlers as a shape. **Needs:** context slots, shapes. **Done when:** logging 1 million lines per second per core adds less than a stated p99 cost to the HTTP benchmark and output matches slog's JSON format.
- [ ] Queue and stream clients: Kafka, NATS, SQS, RabbitMQ, Redis streams
  **Work:** non-blocking clients for the common message systems, written like the redis and mysql clients (per-core connections, tasks parking on `rt_task_wait`, the ambient deadline). **Why:** services need queues as much as databases; Go has mature clients, Tin has none. **How:** start with Redis streams (extends `redis`) and NATS (simple text protocol), then Kafka (binary protocol, partitions, consumer groups), SQS (HTTP plus TLS and AWS signing) and RabbitMQ (AMQP 0-9-1). **Needs:** TLS for managed services; tasks for background consumers. **Done when:** each client passes a CI check against a fake server in the style of `redis_check.py` and against the real service, with throughput published.
  - [x] `kafka`: producer (idempotent, batching, gzip/snappy/lz4/zstd, acks 0/1/all), fetch (read_committed), consumer groups (classic protocol, range and round-robin, static membership), transactions, admin, SASL PLAIN/SCRAM, TLS 1.3, replay (`kafka@1`); `lib/squash` for the codecs. CI check without Kafka: `tests/v2/kafka_broker.tin` (a fake cluster in Tin, in place of a Python fake server: `tools/ci` takes no new Python files); checked by hand against Kafka 3.9 and 4.2 and Java's clients (`notes/stdlib_kafka.md`). Open: throughput published, a CI job against a real broker, KIP-848 groups, OAUTHBEARER.
- [ ] Cloud clients: S3-compatible object storage, GCS, Azure Blob; secrets managers; service discovery
  **Work:** clients for object storage, secret stores and service discovery. **Why:** almost every cloud service reads configuration and stores blobs; without these, Tin services need sidecars. **How:** HTTP client plus TLS, request signing (AWS SigV4 with HMAC-SHA256 from seal), streaming uploads and downloads on the io shapes. **Needs:** TLS, streaming bodies, the io shapes. **Done when:** S3 put/get/list against MinIO in CI and the other services against their emulators.
- [ ] gRPC and protobuf, with derivation instead of reflection
  **Work:** protobuf encoding and decoding derived from Tin types or generated from `.proto` files, and gRPC client and server on HTTP/2. **Why:** gRPC is the standard service-to-service protocol; Go's implementation relies on generated code plus reflection, and Tin's derivation can make encoders as fast as argo's. **How:** derivers for the protobuf wire format, a `.proto` to Tin generator, gRPC framing on the HTTP/2 implementation. **Needs:** derivation, HTTP/2, TLS. **Done when:** interop tests pass against grpc-go's interop server and client.
- [ ] GraphQL, OpenAPI server and client generation
  **Work:** a GraphQL server library and generators from OpenAPI specifications for servers (anvil routes) and clients. **Why:** API-first teams generate code from schemas; matching their workflow eases adoption. **How:** generators in Tin run by `tin generate`, producing typed handlers and argo-encoded types. **Needs:** derivation; code generation tooling. **Done when:** a sample OpenAPI spec generates a server and client that pass a round-trip test, and a GraphQL server passes a reference query suite.
- [ ] Rate limiting, circuit breaking, retries with budgets, hedged requests
  **Work:** resilience primitives as library packages: token-bucket and sliding-window limiters, circuit breakers, retries with budgets and backoff, hedged requests. **Why:** production services need them; per-core state makes them cheap (each core has its own limiter share, no locks). **How:** per-core state with optional cross-core aggregation through atomics; hedging with scopes (first result wins, the other is cancelled). **Needs:** tasks and scopes, atomics. **Done when:** each primitive has tests with a virtual clock and the hedged request cuts p99 in a slow-backend benchmark.
- [ ] Caching: in-process cache with admission policy, distributed cache clients
  **Work:** an in-process cache (per core or one owner core, with TinyLFU-style admission and size limits) and clients for distributed caches beyond redis (memcached). **Why:** caches are where share-nothing needs a pattern (design_foundations section 6: N per-core caches or one owner answering relay requests) and where long-lived memory must be reclaimed (14.1). **How:** entries `keep`-copied into the ingot heap and freed explicitly on eviction under the 14.1 policy; per-core by default. **Needs:** the long-lived heap reclamation policy of 14.1. **Done when:** a cache benchmark shows hit rates matching a reference policy, memory stays bounded over a long soak test, and no lock is used.
- [ ] Metrics and tracing: Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, Datadog formats, exemplars
  **Work:** exporters for the runtime's counters, histograms and spans in the common formats. **Why:** observability is required in production, and section 3 builds the data in the runtime; exporters make it visible to existing systems. **How:** Prometheus text format served by anvil, OTLP over HTTP (protobuf by derivation), Datadog's formats over UDP/HTTP, exemplars linking histogram buckets to trace ids from context slots. **Needs:** runtime observability, protobuf, context slots. **Done when:** each exporter is validated by its official parser or collector in CI.
- [ ] Config: layered configuration, environment, files, hot reload, secrets
  **Work:** configuration loading from defaults, files (JSON, YAML, TOML), environment and flags into a typed struct, with reload. **Why:** every service does this; with derivation it becomes one call that fills a struct with checked attributes. **How:** derivers for each format, merging by layer, reload published to cores through the read-mostly epoch scheme of 14.1. **Needs:** derivation, the epoch/RCU scheme. **Done when:** a struct fills from all layers in tests and a reload is seen by every core without a mutex.
- [ ] Feature flags and experimentation clients
  **Work:** clients for feature flag services and a local evaluator. **Why:** common in product services; evaluation is on the request path, so it must be fast and non-blocking. **How:** flag rules held as read-mostly data updated through the 14.1 scheme, evaluated per request with context slots for user attributes. **Needs:** the epoch scheme, context slots. **Done when:** an evaluator passes the reference test suite of an open flag specification (OpenFeature) and adds negligible latency.
- [ ] Template engines (text and HTML, escaped by construction)
  **Work:** a template engine compiled at build time, with HTML contextual escaping that cannot be bypassed accidentally. **Why:** COVERAGE lists `text/template` and `html/template` as missing; a runtime reflection engine contradicts Tin's design, while compiling templates through derivation gives type-checked templates and generated-code speed. **How:** parse templates at compile time (via `embed` and a deriver), generate code that writes into a buffer, apply escaping by output context in the generated code. **Needs:** derivation, embed. **Done when:** templates with a type error fail at compile time, a corpus of XSS vectors is escaped, and rendering is faster than Go's `html/template`.
- [ ] Search and analytics clients (Elasticsearch, ClickHouse)
  **Work:** clients for search and analytical databases. **Why:** common backends for services; ClickHouse also appears in the drivers list of 12.3. **How:** Elasticsearch over HTTP and JSON (argo), ClickHouse's native protocol or HTTP interface, both pooled per core. **Needs:** HTTP client completeness, TLS. **Done when:** each client passes a CI check against a container of the real service.
- [ ] Audio and media helpers relevant to streaming services (ID3, MP4 boxes, HLS and DASH manifests, Opus/AAC framing)
  **Work:** parsers and writers for media metadata and streaming manifests. **Why:** streaming services (the kind of service used as a yardstick) handle these formats daily; they are parsing-heavy and fit Tin's strengths. **How:** zero-copy parsers over `[]u8` in the request pool, fuzzed (untrusted input), manifests generated with string building. **Needs:** the io shapes for streaming; fuzzing. **Done when:** each parser reads a corpus of real files identically to a reference tool and is fuzzed.
- [ ] Machine-learning inference helpers (tensor layout, ONNX runtime binding) once FFI policy is settled
  **Work:** tensor types and bindings to an inference runtime. **Why:** services increasingly call models in-process; this needs calling C libraries, which waits on the FFI decision. **How:** after the FFI policy (section 11 and 14.2), bind ONNX Runtime's C API behind a capability, with SIMD kernels for pre- and post-processing. **Needs:** the FFI policy, SIMD. **Done when:** a sample model runs from a Tin service with results matching the reference runtime.

### 11. Open questions (decide, then move to a section above)

Each question gets a design note in the format of notes/design_foundations.md (need, decision, replaces, rejected, unlocks), an owner and a deadline (14.5).

- [ ] FFI policy: how Tin calls C libraries without `cgo`, and how capabilities limit it
  **Work:** decide whether and how user code may call C libraries. **Why:** today only `lib/` may declare `extern` functions (LANGUAGE.md section 18); darwin system calls, Windows, sqlite, root certificate stores and ML runtimes all need foreign calls, and 14.2 promotes this to a design note with a date. **How:** options include externs allowed in packages granted an `ffi` or `unsafe` capability, generated bindings from C headers, and region rules for memory handed to C (C must never keep request memory). **Needs:** packages with capabilities. **Done when:** a design note is merged and either an FFI example with capability checks works, or the omission is documented.
- [ ] Generics beyond monomorphization: dictionary passing for code size
  **Work:** decide whether some generic code should be compiled once with a dictionary of operations instead of per type. **Why:** monomorphization gives zero-cost generics but grows code size and compile time with every instantiation (COMPILER.md section 5); shapes and derivation increase instantiations. **How:** measure instantiation counts and sizes on the standard library and real programs; compare against the shared-instantiation approach of section 2 first. **Needs:** shapes; measurements. **Done when:** a note with measurements decides, and the decision is reflected in section 2.
- [ ] Async I/O across cores for file systems that cannot be non-blocking
  **Work:** decide how file I/O on file systems without non-blocking support (most local file systems via read/write, NFS) is done without stalling a core. **Why:** quarry sends file reads and writes to four shared helper threads today, with a 4096-job queue process-wide (RUNTIME.md); a busy disk or slow NFS can fill it. **How:** options are io_uring on Linux (completion-based), a larger per-core helper pool, or the offload pool of 14.1 with deadline-aware queues. **Needs:** the completion-capable I/O layer design (14.2). **Done when:** the decision is written and a test with an artificially slow file system shows fast requests unaffected.
- [ ] Hot code reload for development
  **Work:** decide whether a development mode reloads changed code without restarting the process. **Why:** fast iteration helps adoption; but Tin builds static executables, globals are per core and region checking is whole-program, so reloading code safely is hard. **How:** the likely answer is fast rebuilds plus zero-downtime restart (section 3) rather than in-process patching. **Needs:** compile speed work and graceful restart. **Done when:** the decision is written; if "restart", a `tin run --watch` restarts on change within a stated time.
- [ ] A long-lived arena with explicit drop (not a collector) for graphs that `keep` copies poorly; see 14.1 for reclaiming the long-lived heap
  **Work:** decide whether to add an arena type whose objects live until the arena is dropped as a whole. **Why:** `keep` deep-copies every value into the ingot heap, which is costly for large graphs (a parsed configuration, a routing table, an in-memory index) and leaves the question of freeing them when replaced. **How:** an arena is a region object outside request pools; the region checker treats it as a separate region; dropping it is explicit and is checked so nothing long-lived still points into it (ties to the 14.1 reclamation policy). **Needs:** the 14.1 design note on reclaiming the long-lived heap. **Done when:** a note decides, and if accepted, a router-table or config swap uses an arena with a test that the old one is freed.

### 12. Detailed task breakdown

Every item below is a task a pull request can close. Language features share one template; each feature lists the specific work on top of it.

#### 12.1 The template every language feature follows

These nine steps apply to every feature in 12.2 and section 1; a feature's box is checked only when all nine are done for it.

- [ ] design note updated in notes/design_foundations.md with the final syntax and rules
  **Work:** before code, record the final spelling, typing rules, region rules and rejected alternatives in the design note. **Why:** design_foundations.md section 10 leaves surface syntax to be refined during implementation; writing the result down keeps the specification, docs and tools consistent and makes later reviews possible. **How:** update the feature's section in the same PR series, in the existing format (need, decision, replaces, rejected, unlocks). **Needs:** a prototype where the design is uncertain. **Done when:** the note matches what the compiler accepts, checked by a reviewer against the tests.
- [ ] lexer and parser: grammar, error recovery, positions in diagnostics
  **Work:** add the feature's tokens and grammar to `lex.tin` and `parse.tin`, recover from errors so one mistake does not hide the rest, and report precise positions. **Why:** the compiler reports every error in one run (TOOLING.md section 3), which requires recovery; positions feed the LSP. **How:** new node kinds in `parse.tin` (the source of truth for node layouts), grammar rules added to LANGUAGE.md section 19. **Needs:** the design note. **Done when:** the grammar is in section 19, malformed inputs produce positioned errors in `_bad.tin` tests, and the parser fuzzer finds no crash.
- [ ] checker: typing rules, diagnostics with codes, region/escape rules
  **Work:** type-check the feature in `check.tin`/`lower.tin`, give each new diagnostic a code, and teach `region.tin` the feature's escape behaviour. **Why:** "checked at compile time" is a principle; every new construct is a potential region hole (closures, tasks, slots all are). **How:** lower the feature to existing forms where possible so later passes need no change (COMPILER.md section 11), add region bits and summaries as needed. **Needs:** parser support. **Done when:** typing and region errors have negative tests with exact `.err` output, and the counterexample corpus gains cases for the feature.
- [ ] lowering and code generation on arm64 and amd64
  **Work:** generate code for the feature in both backends (`gen.tin` and `gen_x64.tin`). **Why:** three targets are supported and must stay at parity; a feature on one CPU only splits the language. **How:** prefer lowering to existing node kinds; add backend code only for new primitives, with lit-style checks of the generated instructions. **Needs:** the checker. **Done when:** the feature's tests pass on darwin-arm64, linux-arm64 and linux-amd64, and `make bootstrap` stays a fixed point.
- [ ] runtime support (if any), with allocation and Linux behavior covered
  **Work:** add any runtime functions the feature needs to `lib/runtime/`, with both OS files updated. **Why:** runtime code runs everywhere and must not leak pool memory or differ between macOS and Linux (the OS layer of RUNTIME.md section 8). **How:** keep helpers behind `rt_` names with the same names in both OS files; document them in RUNTIME.md. **Needs:** codegen. **Done when:** runtime behaviour is tested on all targets, including pool reset cycles where memory is involved.
- [ ] tests: positive, negative (`_bad.tin` with `.err`), regression cases tied to issues
  **Work:** tests that show the feature works, that misuse is rejected with exact diagnostics, and that every bug found is pinned. **Why:** the CI policy (docs/CI.md) makes regressions blocking only once a test exists; negative tests guard the checker. **How:** `tests/v2/NAME.tin` with `.out`, `NAME_bad.tin` with `.err`, and `tests/regressions` entries with issue numbers in `cases.json`. **Needs:** the implementation. **Done when:** the feature has at least one positive and one negative test per rule in its design note, all green in CI.
- [ ] docs: docs/LANGUAGE.md section, COVERAGE.md row, examples
  **Work:** document the feature in the language reference, update the COVERAGE row it changes, and add an example. **Why:** COVERAGE says to update it in the same change that adds a capability; LANGUAGE.md is today's specification. **How:** edit the relevant LANGUAGE.md section and the "Differences from Go" table, change the COVERAGE status, add an example under `examples/` when the feature is user-facing. **Needs:** the implementation. **Done when:** the docs describe exactly what the tests exercise and COVERAGE's counts are updated.
- [ ] stdlib adoption: the packages that wait for it (named below) switch to it
  **Work:** convert the standard library packages that the feature unblocks (for example `sift` Func forms to closures, `flume` to io shapes). **Why:** a feature is not proven until the library uses it, and the library is where its performance shows; design_foundations "unlocks" lists name the packages. **How:** one PR per package, with its Go twin re-run. **Needs:** the feature merged. **Done when:** every package named under the feature in 12.2 uses it and its twin still passes.
- [ ] performance check: benchmark against the Go equivalent, no regression in compile time
  **Work:** measure the feature's runtime cost against Go's equivalent and check that compile time did not regress. **Why:** performance is the end goal; features like closures and `dyn` have costs design_foundations promises to keep visible and small. **How:** a micro benchmark per feature (closure call, `dyn` call, scope spawn) next to a Go twin, and the compiler's self-build time (0.07 s warm) compared before and after. **Needs:** the implementation. **Done when:** the numbers are recorded in the PR and in PERFORMANCE.md where relevant, and compile time is within the 2 percent gate.

#### 12.2 Language features

**Closures that capture (#140)**
- [x] closure object layout: code pointer plus captured cells, region-tagged
  **Work:** define the closure's memory layout (code pointer, environment pointer to a table of cell references) and the function-value representation that carries it. **Why:** today a func value is a bare code address (RUNTIME.md section 1); design_foundations section 1 makes a closure a region object like a struct, so `keep` and the region checker treat it uniformly. **How:** a func value becomes two words (code, environment) or one pointer to a closure record; top-level functions get a null environment; calls through func values pass the environment in a fixed register. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** calls through func values work for both top-level functions and closures on both CPUs, and the layout is documented in RUNTIME.md section 1.
- [ ] capture analysis: by value for immutable, cell for mutated variables (open: every captured variable is a cell today, which is correct; copying never-reassigned variables by value is a later optimization)
  **Work:** find which locals each literal uses and put only mutated-and-captured variables into cells, copying never-mutated ones by value. **Why:** design_foundations keeps Go's sharing semantics; copying immutable captures avoids an allocation per variable, which is the cost the design note asks to measure. **How:** a pass over the function body in `check.tin` marking captured symbols and whether any assignment follows capture, then rewriting their uses to cell loads and stores. **Needs:** the layout. **Done when:** a counter closure shares state with its parent, an immutable capture allocates no cell (allocation count test), and loop variables follow the per-iteration rule decided below.
- [x] `keep` of a closure copies its cells into long-lived memory
  **Work:** generate `keep$N` for closures: copy the code pointer and deep-copy every cell's value into the ingot heap. **Why:** a kept closure must own its captures so it can be stored long-term and later run without touching a reset pool; this is the one place Tin differs from Go's semantics, visible at the `keep` (design_foundations section 1). **How:** extend keep generation in `check.tin`; reject keeping a closure that captures something not keepable, naming the variable. **Needs:** capture analysis. **Done when:** a kept closure stored in a global still works after many pool resets, and its parent's later writes are not seen by it (test).
- [x] escape rule: a closure that captures request memory cannot be stored in a global
  **Work:** extend `region.tin` so a closure carries the region bits of its captures and storing it into long-lived memory without `keep` is an error. **Why:** without this rule a closure is a dangling-pointer channel past request reset. **How:** give the closure allocation RG_FRESH plus the bits of captured values; function-value call summaries already join over all functions used as values (COMPILER.md section 6). **Needs:** capture analysis. **Done when:** storing a capturing closure in a global, a map in a global, or a struct reachable from one is a compile error with a `keep` suggestion, in negative tests.
- [x] function literals as arguments to `sift.SortFunc`, `twine.Map`, `FieldsFunc` etc. with capture
  **Work:** make the library's Func-taking functions accept capturing literals and rewrite examples that worked around the limitation. **Why:** this is the main user-visible payoff of closures; today `sift.SortFunc(xs, cmp)` can only use state through globals. **How:** no API change is needed if func types stay one type; check that region summaries let request-local closures be passed down without errors and that non-escaping closures keep cells in the frame. **Needs:** the frame-local optimization for zero cost. **Done when:** sorting by a captured key and `twine.Map` with a captured table work in tests, and generic `sift.SortFunc` with a capturing comparator is no slower than with a top-level one.
- [x] defer with closures; `for` loop variable per-iteration semantics decided and documented
  **Work:** allow `defer func() { ... }()` with captures, and decide whether loop variables are fresh per iteration (Go 1.22 semantics) when captured. **Why:** deferred closures are the usual way to run cleanup with state; the loop-variable rule is a classic bug source that Go changed in 1.22. **How:** `finish_defers` already appends flagged calls before returns; it must save the closure value at the defer point; per-iteration variables mean a fresh cell per iteration only when captured. **Needs:** capture analysis; `defer` in loops (14.2) interacts. **Done when:** the rule is in LANGUAGE.md, and tests show closures created in a loop capture distinct variables and deferred closures see final values.

**Shapes (#141)**
- [x] structural shapes declared with `shape`, satisfied implicitly by methods
  **Work:** parse `shape` declarations (method sets, composition by listing shapes, named unions) and check structural satisfaction. **Why:** structural satisfaction lets the existing library satisfy new shapes without edits (design_foundations section 2), which is why nominal `impl` blocks were rejected. **How:** a new type kind in `types.tin`; satisfaction compares method names, parameter and result types and `mut` marks. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** shapes compose, unions work as constraints, and satisfaction tests cover methods on generic types.
- [x] static dispatch by monomorphization (default) with no run-time cost
  **Work:** let a shape be a type-parameter constraint so calls on a shaped parameter are direct calls in each instantiation. **Why:** "nothing hidden": the default must cost nothing compared to calling the concrete method. **How:** constraints in `generics.tin` accept shapes; method calls on a type parameter resolve at instantiation. **Needs:** shape declarations. **Done when:** a lit-style test shows a direct `bl` to the concrete method and a benchmark shows no difference from a hand-written call.
- [ ] `dyn` fat reference (data pointer plus table) for open sets, with region rules
  Decided (moved from Open questions): the table layout is internal to a whole-program build; no cross-package ABI is promised (notes/design_dyn.md).
