  **Work:** require a regression test in every fixing PR. **Why:** docs/CI.md's policy: a regression becomes required in the fixing PR, and exemptions are visible as XFAIL. **How:** `tests/regressions` with `cases.json` entries carrying the issue number; the issue audit checks exemptions. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** every closed bug issue has a case, checked by the audit.
- [ ] no Python added under tools/ci beyond extending existing files; no Go in the build (Go stays only as a comparison baseline)
  **Work:** keep the build and CI free of new Python tools and of Go. **Why:** Tin is written in Tin; new tooling should be Tin, and existing Python checks may be extended but not multiplied. **How:** review rule; new checks extend existing files; Go is used only for reference programs, conformance tools and benchmarks. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** a release's diff adds no new Python file under `tools/ci` and the build needs no Go.
- [ ] docs regenerate cleanly (`gendoc.py`, `gen_unicode.py`, COVERAGE) and are checked in CI
  **Work:** regenerate generated docs and tables in CI and fail if they differ from the committed ones. **Why:** STDLIB.md, the Unicode tables and COVERAGE drift from the code otherwise. **How:** run the generators in CI and diff (until `tin doc` replaces `gendoc.py`). **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** CI fails on a stale generated file.
- [ ] benchmarks do not regress by more than 2 percent without a written reason
  **Work:** a performance regression gate. **Why:** performance is the end goal; small regressions accumulate. **How:** the benchmark suite of section 4 on dedicated hardware with confidence intervals (14.5); a PR may override with a written reason. **Needs:** dedicated benchmark hardware. **Done when:** the gate runs on every merge and blocks unexplained regressions.

### 13. API-level task list (every exported Go function, type, method and constant group)

Each line is one task: the Go item, what Go documents it as doing (the first sentence of Go's own doc comment), what Tin has today for it, and when it is done. Marks: `[x]` verified against Go (the package has a twin in notes/stdlib_verified.md or is done in docs/COVERAGE.md); `[~]` a Tin function of that name exists but the package is partial or by design, so it is not verified; `[ ]` to do; `[-]` replaced by design, with the replacement named. Constants are one task per package. Packages marked n/a in docs/COVERAGE.md are left out. 'Done when' always means: the generated Go twin program and the Tin test print identical output for this item, including fault messages, and the bug-fix policy (regression case tied to an issue) was followed for anything the twin found.

**5316 API tasks (425 verified, 106 name-only, the rest to do or replaced), plus 497 per-package quality tasks.**

### 14. Review corrections and the work the first draft left out

An independent review of sections 1 to 13 found contradictions with Tin's design (fixed in place above), missing areas, ordering mistakes and oversized items. This section holds what it added; every box is a task.

#### 14.1 Memory the design leaves open
- [ ] Reclaiming the long-lived heap in a server that runs for months: what frees an overwritten global, an evicted cache entry, a replaced config; design note with the rule (explicit drop, epoch reclaim, or arena per owner) and the leak detector
  **Work:** decide and implement how ingot-heap memory is freed when a long-lived value is replaced. **Why:** request memory is wiped per request, but `keep` copies live in the ingot heap and nothing frees them when a global is overwritten (maps free old tables on growth, RUNTIME.md section 3, but kept values are not freed); a months-long server with a cache or config reload grows without bound. **How:** compare explicit `drop` checked by the region checker, epoch-based reclamation (old values freed once every core has passed a quiescent point, natural with share-nothing event loops), and arenas per owner (section 11); write the design note; add a leak detector. **Needs:** nothing to decide; the arena question in section 11 depends on it. **Done when:** the note is merged, the chosen mechanism is implemented, and a cache that replaces entries for hours keeps a flat RSS in a CI soak test.
- [ ] Leak and growth diagnostics: per-core heap statistics, allocation-site sampling for `keep`, a debug mode that reports memory still reachable from globals at shutdown
  **Work:** tools to find long-lived memory growth. **Why:** without a collector, a leak is a `keep` that is never released; users need to see where kept memory comes from. **How:** per-core counters of ingot bytes by size class, sampled call sites for `keep$N` calls (recorded in a heap profile), and a shutdown walk from globals in debug builds listing what is still reachable by type. **Needs:** observability; line tables for site names. **Done when:** a test with a deliberate leak is reported with its `keep` site.
- [ ] Fragmentation policy and a month-long soak test (allocate, keep, drop under a synthetic cache workload; resident size must stay within a stated bound)
  **Work:** state how the ingot heap limits fragmentation and prove it with a long soak test. **Why:** size-class slabs never return memory to the OS today and blocks never cross cores; under churn, fragmentation can grow RSS even without leaks. **How:** a policy (slab release when empty, `madvise`, per-class compaction where possible) and a synthetic workload that allocates, keeps and drops with a realistic size distribution. **Needs:** the reclamation mechanism above; the mmap-based allocator. **Done when:** a month-long run (or an accelerated equivalent) keeps RSS within the stated bound, and a shorter version runs in CI.
- [ ] Read-mostly shared data that changes (config reload, router swap, certificate rotation) without a mutex: an epoch or read-copy-update scheme in the runtime, with the region rules for readers
  **Work:** a runtime mechanism to publish a new version of shared read-only data to every core and free the old version safely. **Why:** anvil's router table is built once and published in a `shared var` before cores start (RUNTIME.md section 9); reloading config, swapping routes or rotating TLS certificates needs replacement at run time, and mutexes are excluded. **How:** an atomic pointer swap of an immutable kept value plus epoch reclamation (each core marks a quiescent point between requests); readers get a reference valid for the current request, and the region checker forbids keeping it past the request. **Needs:** atomics; the memory model; the reclamation design. **Done when:** a router swap under load serves every request from either the old or the new table, the old table is freed after all cores move on, and no lock is taken.
- [ ] Memory model specification: what atomics, `relay` messages and helper-thread results guarantee (happens-before), written as a document and tested on arm64 (weak) and amd64
  **Work:** a written memory model for Tin's few cross-thread mechanisms. **Why:** arm64 is weakly ordered; relay's lock-free queue, helper-thread completions and atomics must give clear happens-before guarantees or cross-core code is subtly wrong. **How:** a short document modelled on Go's memory model but limited to atomics (seq_cst by default), relay send/receive and helper submit/complete; litmus tests run on arm64 hardware. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** the document is in docs and the litmus tests pass on arm64 and amd64 CI runners.
- [ ] Offload pool for CPU-heavy or blocking work (bcrypt, compression, TLS handshakes, file I/O) with a deadline-aware queue, so a core never stalls; acceptance: handshake storm does not move p99 of unrelated requests more than a stated amount
  **Work:** a pool of worker threads for CPU-heavy jobs, with a queue that respects request deadlines. **Why:** cooperative cores stall on long computations; bcrypt and argon2 are slow by design, compression and RSA handshakes are expensive; the four helper threads today serve blocking I/O only. **How:** generalize `rt_helper_run` (heap-owned jobs, completion to the owning core's done pipe, late completions dropped) with priority by deadline, separate limits per job class, and job inputs copied out of request pools. **Needs:** the helper-thread machinery (exists); TLS for the acceptance test. **Done when:** a TLS handshake storm moves the p99 of unrelated plaintext requests by less than the stated amount in a CI benchmark.

#### 14.2 Language and runtime gaps
- [ ] `guard`: unwinding design (run defers on panic, rewind a sub-region, release task resources) and its codegen cost on both CPUs; today a panic ends the process with status 2
  **Work:** design and implement unwinding from a panic to the nearest `guard`. **Why:** `rt_panic` prints a backtrace and exits with status 2 (RUNTIME.md section 7); `guard` (#142) needs to run defers, run cleanup callbacks and rewind the pool without leaving half-updated state visible. **How:** defers are lowered into flagged calls before returns (COMPILER.md section 4), so unwinding needs either per-frame cleanup tables walked by frame pointer or a setjmp-like checkpoint at each guard plus a defer chain recorded at run time; compare cost on both CPUs, choose the one with zero cost on the non-panicking path if possible. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** the design note is merged with measured costs and a guarded panic runs every pending defer in tests on all targets.
- [ ] `defer` inside loops, and the cost model of defers
  **Work:** allow `defer` in loops (with Go's semantics: run at function exit, in reverse order) and document what a defer costs. **Why:** COVERAGE marks `defer` partial ("outside loops"); Go code defers in loops to close files. **How:** a run-time defer list in the frame for defers in loops (allocated in the region), keeping the static flagged form for the rest. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** defers in loops run in Go's order in a twin test and the cost of both forms is in LANGUAGE.md.
- [ ] Struct equality and hashing rules, map key rules for every key type, shadowing rules, written in LANGUAGE.md with tests
  **Work:** write down precise rules for `==` on every type, which types can be map keys and how they hash, and how names shadow each other. **Why:** `==` on structs compares identity while map keys of structs compare by value (LANGUAGE.md sections 3 and 6), a difference users must understand; shadowing rules matter for the linter and the spec. **How:** document current behaviour, fix inconsistencies found, add positive and negative tests per rule. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** LANGUAGE.md has the rules and every rule has a test.
- [ ] Cross-compilation as a first-class command (`tin build -target`), tested from each host to each target
  **Work:** make cross-compiling an explicit, tested feature for every host and target pair. **Why:** the compiler already contains every backend and writes Mach-O and ELF itself (TOOLING.md section 2); this should be guaranteed by tests, not just possible. **How:** CI cross-compiles the test suite from each host to each other target and runs the result on the native runner, comparing with native builds byte for byte. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** CI shows cross builds identical to native builds for all pairs.
- [ ] FFI policy promoted from an open question to a design note with a decision date: how Tin calls system libraries (needed for the darwin system calls and root certificates, Windows, sqlite, ML runtimes) and how capabilities limit it
  **Work:** turn section 11's FFI question into a dated design note. **Why:** several roadmap items wait on it (darwin, Windows, sqlite, ML inference, system root certificates). **How:** the design note in the design_foundations format with an owner and a deadline (14.5). **Needs:** packages with capabilities. **Done when:** the note is merged by its date with a decision.
- [ ] Darwin carve-out for "no libc": macOS requires libSystem for stable system calls; define what is linked and what is replaced
  **Work:** define which libSystem functions Tin keeps on macOS and which it replaces with Tin code. **Why:** macOS does not guarantee a stable system call interface, so raw syscalls are not an option there, unlike Linux. **How:** keep libSystem for system calls, threads and the keychain; replace allocation, formatting, string and math functions with Tin; list each import in RUNTIME.md. **Needs:** the libc removal work on Linux (shared replacements). **Done when:** the list is documented and darwin binaries import only the listed symbols, checked in CI.
- [ ] Completion-capable I/O layer designed before io_uring or IOCP (they are completion-based; epoll and kqueue are readiness-based)
  **Work:** redesign the I/O wait interface so it can sit on readiness (epoll, kqueue) or completion (io_uring, IOCP) backends. **Why:** `rt_task_wait(fd, want, timeout)` waits for readiness and then the caller does the read; completion backends submit the read itself and need buffers owned until completion, which interacts with request pools and deadlines. **How:** a submit-and-wait API (read into a buffer, write from a buffer) implemented on readiness backends by waiting then calling, and natively on completion backends; buffers from heap-owned memory, as helper jobs already are, so expiry is safe. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** the design note is merged and `wire` runs on the new API over epoll and kqueue with no performance loss.
- [ ] Constant-time code generation rules decided before the SSA optimizer lands, and the crypto constant-time tests re-run after every optimizer change
  **Work:** define which optimizations are forbidden in constant-time code and enforce them. **Why:** an optimizer can turn branch-free selection into branches or skip work based on secret values; Tin's tree-walking codegen is predictable today, an SSA optimizer will not be. **How:** a function attribute marking constant-time code, passes that respect it (no branch introduction, no early exits), and the timing tests of section 6 in CI. **Needs:** attributes (#145) for the marker. **Done when:** the rules are documented and the timing tests run after every optimizer change.
- [ ] Editions mechanism before the package registry and before value arrays and the overflow policy (both are breaking changes); versioning and deprecation policy written in year 1, not year 7
  **Work:** schedule the edition mechanism of section 1 early and write versioning and deprecation policy now. **Why:** value arrays and the overflow policy change the meaning of existing code; the registry would spread code written under old rules. **How:** the manifest's edition field and the checker switches of section 1; a policy document. **Needs:** packages (#146). **Done when:** editions exist before either breaking change merges, and the policy is published in year 1.

#### 14.3 Ordering fixes
- [ ] Move `tin fmt` to year 1 (cheap, and stops churn while syntax is still moving)
  **Work:** schedule the formatter of section 5 in year 1. **Why:** a formatter is cheap, removes style churn and enables mechanical rewrites as syntax changes (v0.5 already changed syntax). **How:** reprioritize section 5's item and the comment-preserving parser it needs. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** `tin fmt` ships in a year-1 release and CI checks formatting.
- [ ] Move DWARF line tables, symbolized backtraces and the pprof format to years 1 to 2 (the first production service needs them)
  **Work:** schedule debug info and profiling early. **Why:** operating a production service without file:line backtraces and CPU profiles is impractical; the year-2 exit criterion is a first external service. **How:** reprioritize section 2's DWARF item and section 3's panic and observability items. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** all three ship before the first external production service.
- [ ] Atomics do not depend on tasks: schedule them with the first metrics work, before scopes
  **Work:** reorder atomics ahead of tasks and scopes. **Why:** design_foundations section 9 lists atomics after tasks (step 7, depends on 5), but the `atomic` package itself only needs the existing intrinsics; `hearth.Background` is what needs tasks. **How:** split step 7: atomics now, `hearth.Background` after tasks. **Needs:** the memory model note. **Done when:** the atomic package merges before scopes, and design_foundations section 9 is updated.
- [ ] TLS needs AES and carry-less multiply intrinsics, streaming hashes, `asn1` and `x509`: list them as its prerequisites, in that order
  **Work:** make TLS's dependency chain explicit in the issue tracker and roadmap. **Why:** TLS (#124) is often treated as one item; its prerequisites are large and must land first. **How:** issues for each prerequisite linked from #124, in order. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** #124 lists the prerequisites with issue links and the order is followed.
- [ ] Specification 1.0 and the compatibility promise only after the registry, editions and two external production services
  **Work:** gate 1.0 on real-world validation. **Why:** a compatibility promise made before real use freezes mistakes; section 8 puts spec 1.0 in year 5. **How:** record the gate in the governance document. **Needs:** the registry, editions, production references. **Done when:** the gate is written down and respected.
- [ ] Year 1 is split into 1a (foundations 1 to 3, formatter, benchmark publication) and 1b (foundations 4 to 7, libc removal on Linux, high-demand library packages)
  **Work:** split year 1 into two halves with separate exit criteria. **Why:** year 1 in section 8 holds too much for one milestone; splitting gives a checkpoint. **How:** 1a: closures, shapes, fault chains, `tin fmt`, the v0.4 benchmark published; 1b: io on shapes, tasks, context, atomics, libc removal on Linux, the high-demand packages. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** section 8's table shows 1a and 1b with exit criteria.

#### 14.4 Items too large to be one box (split before scheduling)
- [ ] TLS: record layer; TLS 1.3 client; X.509 path validation; system roots per OS; server; TLS 1.2; session resumption; kernel TLS; conformance with tlsfuzzer and BoGo
  **Work:** split TLS into the listed issues and schedule them in order. **Why:** TLS is months of work with a security-critical result; one box hides progress and risk. **How:** one issue per part with its own acceptance: the record layer against test vectors, the client against real servers, path validation against the x509 limbo suite, the server and 1.2 against BoGo, kTLS against the kernel's tests. **Needs:** 14.3's prerequisite chain. **Done when:** every part has an issue, and the 12.3 TLS item links them.
- [ ] HTTP/2: framing, HPACK, flow control, server push removal, conformance with h2spec; HTTP/3 is a separate project on top of a QUIC stack (loss recovery, congestion control, TLS 1.3 integration) and is not in the first five years
  **Work:** split HTTP/2 into its parts and keep HTTP/3 out of the five-year scope. **Why:** HTTP/2 needs frames, header compression and per-stream flow control in anvil's per-core model; HTTP/3 needs a whole QUIC stack. **How:** issues for framing, HPACK (with its own test vectors), flow control, stream scheduling within a connection's task, and h2spec conformance; no server push (deprecated by browsers). **Needs:** TLS with ALPN. **Done when:** the parts have issues and h2spec passes when they are done.
- [ ] Windows: PE writer, structured exception handling and unwinding, Win32 runtime part, IOCP on the completion-capable layer, path and console semantics, a Windows CI runner
  **Work:** split the Windows target into the listed issues. **Why:** Windows differs in object format, exceptions, system API, I/O model, paths and console handling; each is substantial. **How:** start with a Windows CI runner and a PE writer producing hello world, then the runtime part, then IOCP on the completion-capable layer. **Needs:** FFI policy; the completion-capable layer; guard's unwinding design. **Done when:** each part has an issue and the section 2 Windows item links them.
- [ ] WebAssembly: runtime model without threads, stack switching, file and socket model through WASI, size budget
  **Work:** write the wasm design note covering the listed questions, then split implementation. **Why:** Tin's runtime assumes threads per core and stackful tasks; wasm has neither by default. **How:** the note decides one-core execution, stack switching (proposal or asyncify), the WASI mapping for files and sockets, and a size budget. **Needs:** nothing for the note. **Done when:** the note is merged and implementation issues exist.
- [ ] Regular expressions: parser, Pike VM, one-pass and backtracking engines, lazy DFA, literal acceleration, Unicode classes; each engine verified separately against RE2's corpus
  **Work:** split regexp into separately verified parts. **Why:** each engine has its own bugs; verifying them separately pins failures. **How:** issues per part following 12.3's regexp milestone; a test flag forces each engine. **Needs:** glyph (done). **Done when:** each part has an issue and each engine passes the corpus on its own.
- [ ] Optimizer: SSA construction and verifier; simple passes; bounds-check elimination; register allocation; each lands behind a flag with the whole corpus as the test
  **Work:** split the middle end into the listed steps, each merged behind a flag. **Why:** an optimizer rewrite is the riskiest compiler change; flags let each step be tested on the whole corpus and the bootstrap before it becomes default. **How:** follow 12.4's middle-end list; a flag per pass in `tinc`; CI runs the corpus with each flag on. **Needs:** the constant-time rules (14.2). **Done when:** each step has an issue and lands behind its flag before becoming default.
- [ ] `math/big` with assembly kernels, and the claim "JSON faster than the fastest Go JSON libraries": a baseline and a margin first (see 14.5)
  **Work:** split `math/big` (portable implementation first, kernels later) and turn the JSON claim into a measured target. **Why:** both were stated as single items with unmeasurable goals. **How:** big: Int portable, then Rat and Float, then vector kernels; JSON: pick payloads and libraries, measure today's gap, set a margin. **Needs:** the benchmark suite definition (14.5). **Done when:** issues exist for each part and the JSON target has a number.
- [ ] Formal proofs of the region checker: start with a mechanized core calculus and a soundness statement for it, not the whole language
  **Work:** a small formal model of regions, `keep`, function summaries and closures, with a machine-checked soundness proof. **Why:** proving the whole language is unrealistic; a core calculus captures the key argument and finds design flaws early. **How:** define the calculus in a proof assistant (Coq, Lean or Isabelle), state "no long-lived reference to request memory", prove it; map each checker rule to a calculus rule. **Needs:** closures and tasks designed (they change the calculus). **Done when:** the proof checks and the mapping document links checker code to calculus rules.

#### 14.5 Measurable acceptance criteria (replace the vague items)
- [ ] Define the benchmark suite by name (a list of at least 30 programs with Go baselines), the hardware, and the statistical method (repeat runs, confidence interval); the 2 percent regression gate applies only on dedicated hardware
  **Work:** a named, versioned benchmark list with method and hardware. **Why:** "faster than Go" and "no regression" are meaningless without a fixed suite and statistics; today's bench/v2 has 13 programs measured as best of 3. **How:** extend bench/v2 to at least 30 programs (CPU, allocation, JSON, HTTP, regexp, crypto), fix the machines, use repeated runs with confidence intervals. **Needs:** dedicated runners. **Done when:** the list, hardware and method are documented and the gate uses them.
- [ ] Numbers for "startup time" and "binary size": hello world, an HTTP echo server, the compiler itself, each with a ceiling checked in CI
  **Work:** concrete ceilings for the three programs. **Why:** section 4's budgets need numbers; today hello world is 35 KB and the API server 91 KB on macOS. **How:** measure current values, set ceilings with headroom, check in CI per target. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** ceilings are in PERFORMANCE.md and CI enforces them.
- [ ] "Tin ahead of Go" means: a stated geometric-mean speedup over the suite and no benchmark worse than a stated factor
  **Work:** define the year-3 exit criterion numerically. **Why:** section 8's "Tin ahead of Go on the benchmark suite" needs a number to be checkable. **How:** choose a geometric-mean target and a worst-case factor, recorded with the suite. **Needs:** the suite definition. **Done when:** both numbers are documented and reported for each release.
- [ ] Diagnostics: every error has a stable code and a documented page; "suggestion where one exists" becomes a checklist of error classes that must carry a fix-it
  **Work:** make section 2's diagnostics item measurable. **Why:** "where one exists" is not checkable; a checklist is. **How:** an error-code index with a page per code; a list of classes (missing `mut`, missing `keep`, unhandled fault, missing enum case, shape mismatch, undefined interpolated name) that must carry fix-its, each tested. **Needs:** diagnostic codes. **Done when:** every code has a page and every listed class has a fix-it test.
- [ ] Observability: the list of counters, histograms and span names, and the export formats (Prometheus text, OpenTelemetry), each with a test
  **Work:** name every metric and span the runtime provides. **Why:** section 3's observability item lists kinds, not names; dashboards and alerts need stable names. **How:** a table in RUNTIME.md (requests, waits, helper queue depth, pool bytes, tasks per core, latency histograms) with units and labels; tests that scrape each. **Needs:** runtime observability. **Done when:** the table is published and each entry is tested in both export formats.
- [ ] "Differential fuzzing against Go twins": generate programs from a restricted grammar, run them under Tin and Go, compare output; list the grammar subset
  **Work:** define the subset for section 2's differential fuzzing item. **Why:** the shared subset must be explicit (integer types, strings, slices, maps with sorted printing, structs, enums mapped to Go equivalents). **How:** document the grammar and its mapping to Go; the generator emits both programs from one description. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** the grammar is documented and the fuzzer uses exactly it.
- [ ] Every "decision" item gets an owner field in the issue and a deadline; undecided at the deadline means it is declared out of scope
  **Work:** a process rule for the many "decision" items (complex numbers, named results, labels, init, fallthrough, generic methods, gob, FFI). **Why:** open decisions stall dependent work indefinitely. **How:** each decision issue gets an owner and date; at the date, an undecided item is closed as out of scope and COVERAGE updated. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** every decision item in this roadmap has an issue with owner and deadline.

#### 14.6 Missing areas
- [ ] Binary hardening: position-independent executables, read-only relocations, W^X, BTI and pointer authentication on arm64, CET on amd64, stack protector equivalents
  **Work:** apply standard exploit mitigations to Tin binaries. **Why:** Linux arm64 output is already PIE with `BIND_NOW` (COMPILER.md section 9), but BTI, PAC, CET, RELRO and explicit W^X checks are not documented; memory safety reduces but does not remove the need (standard-library raw code, C libraries). **How:** emit `bti` landing pads and `pac`/`aut` on return addresses on arm64, `endbr64` and shadow-stack compatibility on amd64, mark GOT read-only after binding, verify segment permissions. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** `checksec`-style tooling reports every mitigation on for Linux binaries and the suite passes with them on hardware that enforces BTI.
- [ ] Bootstrap provenance: how the checked-in seed binaries are produced and verified (diverse double compilation), and how a seed is rebuilt from source on a clean machine
  **Work:** document and verify where the seed compilers in `seed/` come from. **Why:** a self-hosting compiler bootstrapped from checked-in binaries could carry a trusting-trust backdoor; supply-chain users need assurance. **How:** document the seed refresh procedure (`make seed` after a fixed point), keep a chain back to the original non-Tin bootstrap, and perform diverse double compilation using an independent build path (for example the legacy-syntax path or a second implementation) to show the seeds match. **Needs:** reproducible builds. **Done when:** the procedure is documented and a DDC run reproduces the current seeds.
- [ ] Release engineering: versioning scheme, changelog generation, backports to supported releases, signed artifacts, an error-code index, versioned documentation
  **Work:** a defined release process. **Why:** releases exist (`make dist`, the installer, versioned images per DISTRIBUTION.md) and `tools/ci/next_version.py` computes versions, but backports, changelogs, signatures and versioned docs are not defined. **How:** document semver-style versioning with editions, generate changelogs from PR titles, keep release branches for supported versions, sign artifacts (section 6), publish docs per version. **Needs:** signed releases. **Done when:** a release is cut following the documented process end to end.
- [ ] Testing: a random program generator for miscompiles (Csmith-like), automatic test-case reduction, miscompile bisection by pass, soak and chaos tests for the scheduler (injected delays, dropped sockets), fuzzing of the region checker for soundness
  **Work:** advanced testing infrastructure. **Why:** miscompiles and scheduler bugs are the hardest to find; the region checker's soundness is a safety property. **How:** a generator producing UB-free programs (Tin has no UB apart from library raw code), a delta-debugging reducer, per-pass disable flags for bisection, fault injection in the runtime (random delays at parks, dropped sockets) for soak runs, and a region fuzzer that generates programs and checks at run time (debug mode, section 6) that no request memory is reached after reset. **Needs:** the sanitizer-grade debug mode; pass flags. **Done when:** each tool runs in a nightly job and has found or ruled out a class of bugs.
- [ ] Documentation: language specification with examples tested by the suite, architecture documents for the compiler and runtime, onboarding guide, glossary
  **Work:** fill documentation gaps for contributors. **Why:** COMPILER.md and RUNTIME.md exist but will age as the compiler gains SSA and the runtime changes; contributors need onboarding and shared vocabulary (ingot, keep, core, relay, shape). **How:** extract spec examples into tests, keep architecture docs updated in the same PRs as changes, write an onboarding guide and glossary. **Needs:** the specification. **Done when:** each document exists and spec examples run in CI.

#### 14.7 Section 13 corrections
- [ ] Extractor: include generic functions and methods (the first version dropped generics, so `slices` and `maps` were almost empty, and `go doc -all` methods were missed)
  **Work:** fix the script that generates section 13 so it includes generic functions and methods. **Why:** section 13 is the API-level checklist; missing generics hid most of `slices` and `maps`. **How:** extend the extractor to parse generic signatures and methods from `go doc -all` output, then regenerate section 13. **Needs:** nothing. **Done when:** section 13 lists every exported generic function and method of `slices`, `maps` and `cmp`, checked against `go doc -all`.
- [ ] Group constants: packages such as `syscall` and `debug/elf` have thousands of constants; one task per constant group, not per name
  **Work:** emit one task per constant group in section 13. **Why:** thousands of single-constant tasks drown the real work. **How:** group by Go's `const (...)` blocks or common prefixes in the extractor. **Needs:** the extractor. **Done when:** section 13's size for `syscall` and `debug/elf` shrinks to grouped tasks.
- [ ] Mark three states: verified (`[x]`), a same-named function exists but the package is partial or by design (`[~]`, not verified), missing (`[ ]`)
  **Work:** a third state in section 13 for functions that exist but are not verified. **Why:** a same-named function is not proof of identical behaviour; only a Go twin earns `[x]` (notes/stdlib_verified.md). **How:** the extractor checks Tin's exported names per package (from `lib/` or STDLIB.md) and the verification record. **Needs:** the extractor. **Done when:** section 13 uses the three states consistently.
- [ ] Mark APIs replaced by design (`[-]` with the replacement named): `reflect` (derivation), `unsafe` (audited raw-memory package), `sync.Mutex` and `RWMutex` (no mutexes), `runtime.GC` and `SetFinalizer` (no collector), `context.WithValue` (typed slots), `errors.As` (sentinels), `net/rpc` and `encoding/gob` (reflection-based), `text/template` and `html/template` (need derivation first), `expvar`, `iter.Pull` (tasks)
  **Work:** mark Go APIs that Tin replaces by design, naming the replacement. **Why:** listing them as missing invites porting what the design rejects (mutexes, `As`, untyped context values). **How:** a table of replacements in the extractor, applied when generating section 13. **Needs:** the extractor. **Done when:** every listed API appears as `[-]` with its replacement.
- [ ] Move the per-package quality tasks to one list (12.5); keep only the Go twin, the regression policy and the benchmark per package, and a fuzz target only for packages that parse untrusted input
  **Work:** reduce section 13's per-package boilerplate. **Why:** repeating identical quality tasks per package adds noise; 12.5 already states the gates. **How:** the extractor emits only the three per-package tasks (twin, regressions, benchmark) and a fuzz task for parsers. **Needs:** the extractor. **Done when:** section 13 has no other repeated quality tasks.
